questions.stem: Why are vegetations in infective endocarditis particularly prone to causing septic infarcts?

options.A: They are calcified and cannot fragment
options.B: They are friable and emboli can carry many organisms to distant tissues
options.D: They remain confined to the valve annulus

questions.explanation: IE vegetations are friable. When fragments embolize, they carry organisms and can seed infected infarcts or abscesses.

questions.stem: Which peripheral finding is correctly paired with its typical pain characteristic?

options.B: Osler node — painless lesion on palm or sole
options.C: Janeway lesion — painless lesion on palm or sole

questions.explanation: Janeway lesions are painless lesions on palms/soles, whereas Osler nodes are painful fingertip nodules.

questions.stem: Culture-negative infective endocarditis may occur because of which factor?
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that culture-negative IE can result from prior antibiotics or organisms that are difficult to isolate.

questions.stem: Which complication of infective endocarditis results from immune-complex deposition rather than direct septic embolization?
questions.explanation: Glomerulonephritis occurs through glomerular trapping of antigen–antibody complexes and may cause hematuria, albuminuria or renal failure.

questions.stem: Which description best fits nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE)?

options.A: Bulky infected vegetations with destructive inflammation
options.B: Small sterile nondestructive vegetations associated with hypercoagulable states
options.C: Vegetations containing abundant bacteria in all cases
options.D: Vegetations found only on prosthetic valves

questions.explanation: NBTE consists of small sterile thrombi, usually on previously normal valves, commonly in hypercoagulable states such as malignancy.

questions.stem: Which underlying condition is especially associated with nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis?
questions.explanation: Malignancy—especially mucinous adenocarcinoma—is emphasized as the most common cause of the hypercoagulable setting behind NBTE.

questions.stem: Libman–Sacks endocarditis is most closely associated with which disease?
questions.explanation: Libman–Sacks is a sterile inflammatory valvular lesion of SLE and can also be seen with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes Libman–Sacks endocarditis from classic NBTE in the lecture?

options.A: It is always caused by S. aureus
options.B: It is associated with inflammation and may show fibrinoid necrosis next to the vegetation
options.D: Its vegetations are confined to the tricuspid valve

questions.explanation: Libman–Sacks lesions are sterile but have associated inflammation, often with fibrinoid necrosis, and chronic fibrosis may deform valves.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man who injects drugs develops high fever and rapidly destructive endocarditis. Which valve and organism pairing is most characteristic?

options.D: Aortic valve — Candida is always required

questions.explanation: IV drug use is strongly associated with S. aureus acute IE, and the tricuspid valve is a classic site in IV drug users.
questions.formative_reference: Endocarditis 2026-2027 lecture clinical application

questions.stem: A patient with known valvular disease develops weeks of fatigue, weight loss and a low-grade illness after a dental procedure. Blood cultures grow viridans streptococci. Which form of endocarditis best fits?

options.A: Acute IE on a normal valve
options.B: Subacute IE on a damaged valve

questions.explanation: Viridans-group streptococci are oral flora classically associated with subacute infective endocarditis on previously damaged valves. The group contains multiple species.
questions.formative_reference: Endocarditis 2026-2027 lecture clinical application
questions.review_note: Viridans streptococci are a group rather than one species named Streptococcus viridans.

questions.stem: A patient with infective endocarditis develops a new conduction abnormality. Which complication should be suspected from the lecture?

options.A: Extension into underlying myocardium with a ring abscess

questions.explanation: New arrhythmias/conduction problems can suggest extension of infection into the underlying myocardium and conduction system, including ring abscess formation.
questions.formative_reference: Endocarditis 2026-2027 lecture clinical application

questions.stem: A patient with endocarditis has painless erythematous lesions on the palms and soles. What are these lesions called?
questions.explanation: Janeway lesions are painless lesions on the palms and soles; Osler nodes are painful fingertip nodules.
questions.formative_reference: Endocarditis 2026-2027 lecture clinical application

questions.stem: A patient with advanced mucinous adenocarcinoma develops multiple systemic infarcts. Echocardiography shows small sterile vegetations on previously normal valves without valve destruction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of malignancy, hypercoagulability, small sterile nondestructive vegetations and systemic emboli is classic NBTE.
questions.formative_reference: Endocarditis 2026-2027 lecture clinical application

questions.stem: A woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has sterile vegetations involving both valve surfaces with adjacent inflammatory injury and fibrinoid necrosis. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Sterile vegetations in SLE with associated inflammation/fibrinoid necrosis are characteristic of Libman–Sacks endocarditis.
questions.formative_reference: Endocarditis 2026-2027 lecture clinical application

lecture_sets.subject: Physiology
lecture_sets.title: Normal ECG
lecture_sets.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

questions.stem: Which cardiac property cannot be directly assessed from a surface ECG?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that ECG evaluates electrical properties but not force of contraction or ejection fraction.

questions.stem: A depolarization wave moving toward the positive exploring electrode produces:
questions.explanation: Depolarization moving toward the positive electrode gives a positive/upward ECG deflection.

questions.stem: A repolarization wave moving away from the positive electrode produces:
questions.explanation: For repolarization, movement away from the positive electrode produces a positive/upward deflection.

questions.stem: The P wave represents:
questions.explanation: The P wave represents atrial depolarization.

questions.stem: The QRS complex represents:
questions.explanation: QRS is ventricular depolarization; atrial repolarization is usually hidden within it.

questions.stem: Why is atrial repolarization usually not visible on the ECG?

options.A: It occurs with ventricular depolarization and is masked by the larger QRS
options.D: It is identical to the T wave

questions.explanation: Atrial repolarization overlaps ventricular depolarization and is obscured by the larger QRS complex.

questions.stem: A PR interval longer than 0.20 s most directly suggests:
questions.explanation: The normal PR interval is about 0.12–0.20 s; prolongation indicates conduction delay/block.

questions.stem: A QRS duration of 0.16 s suggests:
questions.explanation: Normal QRS is under 0.12 s; widening suggests delayed ventricular conduction such as bundle branch block.

questions.stem: Which ECG interval includes both ventricular depolarization and repolarization?
questions.explanation: The QT interval spans ventricular depolarization through repolarization.

questions.stem: A prolonged QT interval increases the risk of:
questions.explanation: The lecture links prolonged QT to ventricular arrhythmias, particularly torsades de pointes.

questions.stem: At 25 mm/s, how many large ECG squares equal one second?
questions.explanation: At standard speed, five large horizontal squares equal one second.

questions.stem: A regular rhythm has 4 large squares between consecutive R waves. The approximate heart rate is:
questions.explanation: For regular rhythm, rate ≈ 300 divided by large squares between R waves: 300/4 = 75/min.

questions.stem: Which finding is required for normal sinus rhythm in this lecture?

options.A: Each P wave is followed by a QRS and each QRS is preceded by a P wave

questions.explanation: Normal sinus rhythm is regular, 60–100/min, with a P before every QRS and normal PR/QRS durations.

questions.stem: Which leads are used in the lecture's quick approach to estimating the electrical axis?
questions.explanation: Lead I and aVF view the heart near 0° and +90° and are used to estimate axis.

questions.stem: The normal electrical axis range given in the lecture is approximately:
questions.explanation: The lecture gives a normal axis from about −30° to +90°.

questions.stem: Which myocardial function cannot be evaluated directly by an ECG?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that ECG evaluates automaticity, conductivity and excitability, but not contractility or ejection fraction.

questions.stem: An ECG represents which of the following?

options.B: The summed electrical activity of many myocardial cells detected at the body surface

questions.explanation: An ECG is not a single action potential; it is the summed electrical activity of many myocardial cells as it spreads through the heart.

questions.stem: Which leads are the standard bipolar limb leads?
questions.explanation: Leads I, II and III are the standard bipolar limb leads.

questions.stem: A depolarization wave moving toward the positive exploring electrode produces which ECG deflection?
questions.explanation: Depolarization moving toward the positive electrode gives an upward/positive deflection.

questions.stem: A repolarization wave moving toward the positive exploring electrode produces which ECG deflection?
questions.explanation: Repolarization moving toward the positive electrode produces a negative/downward deflection.

questions.stem: What does the P wave represent?
questions.explanation: The P wave represents atrial depolarization.

questions.stem: What does the QRS complex represent?
questions.explanation: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization.

questions.stem: What does the T wave represent?
questions.explanation: The T wave represents ventricular repolarization.

questions.stem: Why is atrial repolarization normally not visible on the ECG?

options.B: It occurs during ventricular depolarization and is masked by the larger QRS complex
options.D: It is recorded as the U wave

questions.explanation: Atrial repolarization occurs at the same time as ventricular depolarization and is masked by the much larger QRS complex.

questions.stem: The PR interval normally lasts approximately:
questions.explanation: The lecture gives a normal PR interval of 0.12–0.20 seconds.

questions.stem: A normal QRS complex should generally be:
questions.explanation: The lecture states that normal QRS duration is less than 0.12 seconds.

questions.stem: Which ECG interval includes both ventricular depolarization and ventricular repolarization?
questions.explanation: The QT interval represents ventricular depolarization plus repolarization.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the T wave is usually in the same general direction as the QRS complex?

options.A: Depolarization and repolarization travel in exactly the same direction with the same polarity
options.B: Repolarization travels in the opposite direction and has opposite polarity, producing the same net ECG direction
options.C: The T wave is generated by atrial repolarization
options.D: The T wave is always inverted

questions.explanation: The lecture explains that ventricular repolarization is opposite in direction to depolarization and also opposite in polarity; opposite plus opposite gives the same net direction.

questions.stem: For a regular rhythm, heart rate can be estimated by dividing 300 by:

options.A: The number of small squares in the P wave
options.B: The number of large squares between consecutive R waves
options.C: The number of P waves in 1 second
options.D: The number of QRS complexes in 1 minute of paper

questions.explanation: For a regular rhythm, the lecture uses the rule of 300: 300 divided by the number of large squares between R waves.

questions.stem: A regular ECG has 4 large squares between consecutive R waves. What is the approximate heart rate?
questions.explanation: Using the rule of 300: 300 ÷ 4 = 75 beats/min.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: An ECG shows a PR interval of 0.24 seconds. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.B: Delayed AV conduction / first-degree AV block pattern

questions.explanation: The lecture states that a prolonged PR interval indicates conduction delay or block; the companion ECG lecture links a long PR interval to first-degree heart block.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: An ECG shows a QRS duration of 0.16 seconds. What does this most strongly suggest?

options.B: Delayed ventricular conduction such as bundle branch block

questions.explanation: A QRS wider than 0.12 seconds suggests delayed ventricular conduction, such as bundle branch block.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: A patient has an irregular rhythm. Which heart-rate method from the lecture is appropriate?

options.B: Count R waves in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10
options.C: Count P waves in one small square

questions.explanation: For irregular rhythms, the lecture recommends the six-second method: count R waves in 30 large squares and multiply by 10.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: An ECG has ST-segment elevation. Which type of process does the lecture associate with this finding?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that ST elevation or depression can indicate myocardial ischemia/injury, and its companion lecture associates ST elevation with myocardial infarction.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

lecture_sets.subject: Biochemistry
lecture_sets.title: Diagnostic Cardiac Markers
lecture_sets.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

questions.stem: Which cardiac markers are preferred for diagnosis of myocardial damage and acute coronary syndrome, especially when ECG changes are unclear?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies cTnI and cTnT as the preferred biomarkers for myocardial damage and ACS.

questions.stem: Which statement about cardiac troponin I is emphasized in the lecture?

options.A: It is normally abundant in serum
options.B: It is also strongly expressed in skeletal muscle
options.C: It has not been reported to be expressed in skeletal muscle and is highly specific for cardiac damage
options.D: It returns to normal within 2 hours

questions.explanation: The lecture notes that cTnI has not been reported in skeletal muscle, making it highly specific for cardiac injury.

questions.stem: In the traditional conventional-assay teaching model, cardiac troponin typically becomes detectable after approximately which interval?
questions.explanation: These are traditional conventional-assay teaching comparisons. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin is preferred for current myocardial-injury assessment; early detection varies with the assay and clinical timing. Myoglobin lacks cardiac specificity.
questions.review_note: Qualify older kinetics so they do not override modern high-sensitivity troponin assessment.

questions.stem: Which marker is particularly useful for detecting reinfarction because it returns to normal in about 2–3 days?
questions.explanation: CK-MB returns to normal in 2–3 days, so a new rise can help detect reinfarction.

questions.stem: In traditional comparisons with conventional troponin assays, which marker rises early but is limited by poor cardiac specificity?
questions.explanation: These are traditional conventional-assay teaching comparisons. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin is preferred for current myocardial-injury assessment; early detection varies with the assay and clinical timing. Myoglobin lacks cardiac specificity.
questions.review_note: Qualify older kinetics so they do not override modern high-sensitivity troponin assessment.

questions.stem: A serum LDH-1 level higher than LDH-2 is called which pattern?
questions.explanation: A predominance of LDH-1 over LDH-2 is the classic 'flipped' pattern associated with myocardial injury, although LDH is no longer routinely used.

questions.stem: Which biomarker is released by ventricular cardiomyocytes in response to stretch and is used as a marker of congestive heart failure?
questions.explanation: BNP and NT-proBNP are released in response to ventricular stretch and are used as markers of heart failure.

questions.stem: Which statement about troponin elevation is correct?

options.A: It occurs only in myocardial infarction
options.B: It indicates myocardial injury but can rise in several cardiac and non-cardiac conditions
options.C: It is always caused by skeletal muscle trauma
options.D: It is not useful in ACS

questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes that troponins are markers of cardiac muscle damage, not exclusively myocardial infarction; they can rise in myocarditis, PE, sepsis and other conditions.

questions.stem: Which marker is more sensitive than CK-MB but may give false-positive results with skeletal muscle injury and renal failure?
questions.explanation: Myoglobin is relatively sensitive and rises early, but skeletal muscle injury and renal failure can produce false positives.

questions.stem: Which marker can remain elevated for days after MI and therefore helps with late diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Troponin I stays elevated about 5–10 days and troponin T about 5–14 days, supporting late diagnosis.

questions.stem: A man presents with chest pain after an unusually strenuous day digging in the garden. Total CK is 300 U/L, CK-MB is normal, and troponin T after 12 hours is normal. What is the best interpretation?

options.A: Acute myocardial infarction is strongly supported
options.B: The raised total CK is more consistent with skeletal muscle injury
options.C: Troponin T is expected to be normal in MI
options.D: CK-MB is the least cardiac-specific marker in this case

questions.explanation: The lecture case concludes that the elevated total CK reflected skeletal muscle injury from unaccustomed exercise; normal CK-MB and troponin argued against MI.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: A patient presents 7 days after a suspected myocardial infarction. Which marker is most likely still elevated and therefore useful for late diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Troponins remain elevated for several days; CK-MB and myoglobin usually return to normal much earlier.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: A patient had an MI 4 days ago and now develops new ischemic chest pain. Which marker is useful for identifying reinfarction by showing a new rise?
questions.explanation: Because CK-MB generally returns to normal within 2–3 days, a new increase can support reinfarction.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: In the traditional conventional-assay comparison, which listed marker can rise within about two hours but lacks cardiac specificity?
questions.explanation: These are traditional conventional-assay teaching comparisons. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin is preferred for current myocardial-injury assessment; early detection varies with the assay and clinical timing. Myoglobin lacks cardiac specificity.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case
questions.review_note: Qualify older kinetics so they do not override modern high-sensitivity troponin assessment.

questions.stem: A patient with severe sepsis has elevated cardiac troponin without classic MI findings. Which statement best fits the lecture?

options.B: Troponin indicates myocardial injury and can rise in severe infection

questions.explanation: Severe infection (sepsis) is listed among non-cardiac conditions that can cause myocardial injury and troponin elevation.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

lecture_sets.subject: Pharmacology
lecture_sets.title: Antiarrhythmic Drugs
lecture_sets.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

questions.stem: Which Vaughan Williams class primarily blocks fast sodium channels?
questions.explanation: Class I antiarrhythmics are sodium-channel blockers that slow conduction in fast-response tissue.

questions.stem: Which class prolongs repolarization mainly by blocking potassium channels?
questions.explanation: Class III drugs block potassium channels, prolonging repolarization and refractory period.

questions.stem: A stable patient has a regular narrow-complex SVT dependent on the AV node. Which drug is the lecture's rapid AV-node 'off switch'?
questions.explanation: Adenosine briefly blocks AV nodal conduction and is used for AV-node-dependent re-entrant SVT.

questions.stem: Why must adenosine be given as a rapid IV bolus?

options.A: It has a half-life of about 10 seconds
options.C: It is poorly absorbed from muscle

questions.explanation: Adenosine has an extremely short half-life of about 10 seconds, so rapid IV administration is required.

questions.stem: Which condition is a major contraindication to adenosine in this lecture?
questions.explanation: Adenosine may cause bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma.

questions.stem: A haemodynamically stable patient with preserved left ventricular systolic function has atrial fibrillation with a rapid narrow-complex ventricular response and no pre-excitation. Which listed rate-control strategy is appropriate?

options.A: Beta blocker or non-DHP calcium-channel blocker

questions.explanation: For atrial fibrillation, the lecture uses beta blockers or non-DHP calcium-channel blockers to slow AV nodal conduction for rate control.
questions.review_note: Non-DHP calcium-channel blockers are inappropriate in significant LV systolic dysfunction; supply the necessary setting.

questions.stem: A wide, regular tachycardia should be considered which rhythm until proven otherwise?
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes that a wide-complex tachycardia should be treated as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A patient has sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse, causing hypotension and confusion. What is the immediate rhythm treatment?
questions.explanation: Haemodynamically unstable monomorphic VT with a pulse is treated with synchronized cardioversion. Polymorphic VT cannot be reliably synchronized and requires an unsynchronized high-energy shock; pulseless VT/VF requires defibrillation and CPR.
questions.review_note: Polymorphic VT needs an unsynchronized shock even with a pulse; specify an unstable synchronized-shock rhythm.

questions.stem: Which drug is specifically highlighted for torsades de pointes?
questions.explanation: Magnesium suppresses early afterdepolarizations and is used for torsades de pointes.

questions.stem: Which class reduces sympathetic effects, automaticity, and AV nodal conduction?
questions.explanation: Class II beta blockers reduce sympathetic cardiac effects, decreasing automaticity and AV nodal conduction.

questions.stem: Verapamil and diltiazem belong to which Vaughan Williams class?
questions.explanation: Non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers are Class IV antiarrhythmics and slow AV nodal conduction.

questions.stem: Which Class I subgroup causes moderate sodium-channel block and increases action-potential duration?
questions.explanation: Class IA has moderate sodium-channel block and also prolongs action-potential duration.

questions.stem: Which adverse effect is especially associated with procainamide in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Procainamide can cause a lupus-like syndrome, especially in slow acetylators.

questions.stem: A patient has very fast irregular wide-complex AF with WPW. Which AV-nodal blocker should be avoided?

options.D: None; AV nodal blockade is preferred

questions.explanation: In pre-excited AF, AV-nodal blockers such as adenosine can favor rapid accessory-pathway conduction and should be avoided.

questions.stem: What is the key electrophysiologic effect of Class IC drugs such as flecainide?

options.A: Strong slowing of conduction with little effect on AP duration
options.B: Marked shortening of AV nodal refractory period

questions.explanation: Class IC drugs strongly block sodium channels and markedly slow conduction with little effect on action-potential duration.

questions.stem: Which Vaughan Williams class consists primarily of sodium-channel blockers?
questions.explanation: Class I antiarrhythmics are sodium-channel blockers and are subdivided into IA, IB and IC.

questions.stem: Which class primarily reduces sympathetic effects, automaticity and AV nodal conduction?
questions.explanation: Class II drugs are beta blockers; they reduce sympathetic effects, automaticity and AV nodal conduction.

questions.stem: Which class primarily blocks potassium channels and prolongs repolarization and refractory period?
questions.explanation: Class III drugs block potassium channels and prolong repolarization/refractoriness.

questions.stem: Adenosine terminates many AV-node-dependent re-entry SVTs mainly by:

options.A: Producing a brief AV nodal block

questions.explanation: Adenosine activates A1 receptors, lowers cAMP, increases potassium conductance and produces a transient AV nodal block.

questions.stem: Which drug is particularly useful for ventricular arrhythmias in ischemic myocardium and is given intravenously because of extensive first-pass metabolism?
questions.explanation: Lidocaine is a Class IB drug that preferentially acts on abnormal/inactivated sodium channels in ischemic ventricular tissue and is used IV.

questions.stem: Which Class IC drug should be avoided after myocardial infarction or in significant structural heart disease because of proarrhythmic risk?
questions.explanation: Flecainide is a Class IC drug and is contraindicated after MI/structural disease because of proarrhythmic risk.

questions.stem: Which adverse effect is particularly important with chronic amiodarone therapy?
questions.explanation: The lecture highlights pulmonary toxicity/fibrosis as a serious amiodarone adverse effect, along with thyroid, liver, skin and eye toxicity.

questions.stem: Combining a beta blocker with verapamil or diltiazem increases the risk of:
questions.explanation: Both suppress SA/AV nodal activity, so the combination can cause additive bradycardia and AV block.

questions.stem: Which treatment is specifically associated with torsades de pointes in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes magnesium sulfate for torsades de pointes, along with correction of electrolytes and removal of QT-prolonging causes.

questions.stem: A stable 24-year-old has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190/min. Vagal maneuvers fail. Which drug is the best next step from the lecture?
questions.explanation: For a stable regular narrow-complex AV-node-dependent SVT, adenosine is used after vagal maneuvers fail.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: A patient with WPW develops a stable, very fast irregular wide-complex tachycardia. Which drug is appropriate?
questions.explanation: In stable pre-excited AF with WPW, the lecture recommends procainamide and warns against isolated AV-nodal blockers.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: A patient with prior MI and ventricular scar needs rhythm maintenance for paroxysmal AF. Which drug should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Class IC agents such as flecainide should be avoided after MI or in significant structural disease.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: A patient on chronic amiodarone develops progressive dry cough, dyspnea and diffuse interstitial infiltrates. What is the most likely adverse effect?
questions.explanation: Amiodarone can cause pulmonary pneumonitis/fibrosis, one of its most serious toxicities.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: A patient with HFrEF (EF 30%) needs pharmacologic maintenance of sinus rhythm for AF. Which is a reasonable option from the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture notes amiodarone or dofetilide as rhythm-control options in HFrEF, while Class IC drugs and verapamil are inappropriate.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: A patient has symptomatic sinus bradycardia with HR 32/min, hypotension and dizziness. What is the initial drug?
questions.explanation: The lecture's clinical case identifies atropine as the initial drug for symptomatic bradycardia.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: A patient is pulseless with ventricular fibrillation. What is the most important immediate treatment?
questions.explanation: For pulseless VT/VF, the lecture emphasizes defibrillation and CPR first; antiarrhythmic drugs are adjuncts.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: A patient has polymorphic VT with prolonged-QT physiology and a twisting QRS pattern. Which drug should be given?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies torsades de pointes as a prolonged-QT polymorphic VT treated with magnesium sulfate.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: A patient with hyperthyroidism has atrial fibrillation and marked adrenergic symptoms. Which drug is especially useful initially?
questions.explanation: The lecture highlights beta blockers, including propranolol, for arrhythmias driven by sympathetic activation and hyperthyroidism.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case

questions.stem: A patient has ischaemic chest pain, a blood pressure of 70/40 mmHg and a regular wide-complex rhythm consistent with monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. A pulse is present. Which immediate intervention is indicated?
questions.explanation: Haemodynamically unstable monomorphic VT with a pulse is treated with synchronized cardioversion. Polymorphic VT cannot be reliably synchronized and requires an unsynchronized high-energy shock; pulseless VT/VF requires defibrillation and CPR.
questions.formative_reference: Lecture-grounded clinical/application case
questions.review_note: Polymorphic VT needs an unsynchronized shock even with a pulse; specify an unstable synchronized-shock rhythm.

questions.stem: A febrile patient has a regular heart rate of 118/min with a normal P wave before every QRS. Which rhythm best fits?
questions.explanation: Sinus tachycardia originates in the SA node, exceeds 100/min, and retains P waves before QRS complexes. Fever is a listed trigger.

questions.stem: An athlete at rest has a regular rate of 52/min and a P wave preceding each QRS. Which mechanism can explain this sinus rhythm?
questions.explanation: Vagal activity slows SA-node impulse generation, producing sinus bradycardia with preserved atrioventricular sequencing.

questions.stem: In respiratory sinus arrhythmia, how does the sinus rate usually change with inspiration?

options.B: It becomes an independent ventricular rhythm

questions.explanation: The lecture describes an increased heart rate during inspiration and a reduced rate during expiration.

questions.stem: A premature beat has a differently shaped P wave followed by a normal QRS complex. Where does the ectopic impulse most likely arise?

options.B: Only within the bundle of Kent

questions.explanation: Atrial extrasystoles arise from an atrial ectopic focus; altered P-wave morphology precedes a usually normal QRS.

questions.stem: A premature broad, bizarre QRS is not preceded by a P wave and is followed by a compensatory pause. What is the best description?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies an ectopic ventricular beat by its abnormal QRS, absent preceding P wave, and compensatory pause.

questions.stem: An ECG has a saw-toothed atrial baseline and regular QRS intervals. Which rhythm is most likely?
questions.explanation: Organized rapid atrial activity in flutter produces saw-tooth waves; a fixed AV conduction ratio can produce a regular ventricular rhythm.

questions.stem: A patient has no discrete P waves, fine fibrillatory activity, and irregularly spaced QRS complexes. Which rhythm is most likely?
questions.explanation: The lecture describes absent P waves, fine atrial waves, and irregular QRS intervals in atrial fibrillation.

questions.stem: Which impulse-generation pattern is described for atrial fibrillation?

options.B: Normal sinus impulses with a fixed prolonged PR
options.C: A single delayed impulse from the AV node
options.D: Rapid disorganized activity from multiple atrial foci

questions.explanation: The lecture contrasts multiple rapidly and irregularly discharging atrial foci in fibrillation with more organized flutter activity.

questions.stem: A sinus impulse forms normally but fails to propagate from the SA node to the atria for one beat. Which abnormality is described?
questions.explanation: SA nodal block is a propagation failure between the SA node and atria, rather than delayed AV conduction.

questions.stem: Every P wave is followed by a QRS, but the PR interval is consistently 240 ms. Which conduction abnormality is present?
questions.explanation: First-degree AV block delays conduction while all atrial impulses still reach the ventricles; PR exceeds 200 ms.

questions.stem: The PR interval lengthens progressively until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, then the cycle repeats. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explanation: Progressive PR prolongation before a dropped ventricular beat is the Wenckebach (Mobitz I) pattern.

questions.stem: Some P waves are not conducted, while the PR interval of conducted beats remains constant. Which AV block pattern is most likely?
questions.explanation: Mobitz II causes intermittent nonconducted P waves without the progressive PR prolongation of Mobitz I.

questions.stem: Which conduction tissue is most commonly implicated in the lecture description of Mobitz II block?
questions.explanation: The lecture distinguishes distal His–Purkinje disease in Mobitz II from predominantly AV-nodal disease in Mobitz I.

questions.stem: A patient has a slow ventricular escape rhythm with P waves and QRS complexes occurring independently. Which diagnosis best explains this?
questions.explanation: Complete AV block prevents atrial impulses from conducting to the ventricles, creating AV dissociation and an escape rhythm.

questions.stem: Which ECG relation distinguishes complete AV block from first-degree AV block?

options.A: All P waves conduct with a constant prolonged PR
options.B: Normal P waves precede every QRS at a faster sinus rate
options.C: No fixed relationship between P waves and QRS complexes

questions.explanation: Third-degree block separates atrial and ventricular rhythms; first-degree block preserves one-to-one conduction.

questions.stem: An ECG has a short PR interval and a slurred initial QRS upstroke (delta wave). Which structure explains this pre-excitation?
questions.explanation: An accessory atrioventricular pathway bypasses normal AV-nodal delay and produces ventricular pre-excitation in WPW.

questions.stem: A patient with raised serum potassium has narrow, tall, peaked T waves. Which electrolyte disturbance fits this early ECG finding?
questions.explanation: Tall peaked T waves are an early hyperkalemic change described in the lecture.

questions.stem: With severe hyperkalemia, which additional ECG change can develop?

options.A: A prominent U wave with a flattened T wave
options.B: QRS widening that may merge with T waves into a sine-wave pattern
options.C: An isolated short QT with unchanged QRS
options.D: A consistently prolonged PR with every other feature normal

questions.explanation: Severe hyperkalemia slows ventricular conduction; marked QRS widening may merge with repolarization into a sine-wave pattern.

questions.stem: A patient has flattened T waves and prominent U waves after a fall in serum potassium. Which disturbance is most likely?
questions.explanation: The lecture associates hypokalemia with flattened T waves and prominent U waves.

questions.stem: How does hypercalcemia usually affect the QT interval in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia shortens the QT interval, mainly through shortening of the ST segment.

questions.stem: An ECG shows QT prolongation in a patient with low serum calcium. Which explanation fits the lecture?

options.A: Hypocalcemia lengthens ventricular repolarization, especially the ST segment
options.B: An accessory pathway shortens AV conduction
options.D: Low calcium produces a obligatory saw-tooth baseline

questions.explanation: Hypocalcemia is associated with a longer ST segment and QT interval.

lecture_sets.subject: Anatomy & Histology
lecture_sets.title: Normal Development of Heart & it’s Great Vessels

questions.stem: The primary heart field arises mainly from which embryonic tissue?
questions.explanation: The lecture locates the cardiogenic field in splanchnic lateral plate mesoderm during the third week.

questions.stem: Which embryonic folding movement brings the two endocardial tubes together to form a single heart tube?
questions.explanation: Lateral folding brings the paired cardiac tubes together so that they fuse, except at their caudal ends.

questions.stem: Disappearance of the dorsal mesocardium creates which space?
questions.explanation: The dorsal mesocardium disappears, leaving the transverse pericardial sinus between the arterial and venous ends of the heart.

questions.stem: Which layer of the early heart tube forms its endothelial lining?
questions.explanation: The inner endothelial layer forms endocardium; surrounding myoblasts form myocardium with cardiac jelly between them.

questions.stem: During normal cardiac looping, in which direction does the cephalic part of the tube bend?

options.A: Ventrally, caudally, and to the right
options.B: Dorsally, cranially, and to the left

questions.explanation: The lecture describes rightward bending of the cephalic part during looping, approximately days 23–28.

questions.stem: An embryo is examined during days 23–28. Which major event normally rearranges the straight heart tube into its chamber configuration?

options.D: Final closure of the foramen ovale

questions.explanation: Cardiac looping occurs during this period; fetal-shunt closures occur after birth.

questions.stem: The primitive ventricle mainly forms which adult region?
questions.explanation: The primitive ventricle becomes the rough or trabeculated part of the left ventricle.

questions.stem: The proximal bulbus cordis mainly forms which region?
questions.explanation: The proximal bulbus cordis gives rise to the trabeculated right ventricle.

questions.stem: The conus cordis contributes to which adult structures?

options.A: Smooth outflow regions of both ventricles

questions.explanation: The conus forms the aortic vestibule of the left ventricle and the infundibulum of the right ventricle.

questions.stem: The truncus arteriosus contributes mainly to which structures?
questions.explanation: The distal bulbus (truncus arteriosus) forms the proximal great arterial outlets.

questions.stem: A developmental model traces the smooth-walled sinus venarum of the right atrium. Which embryonic structure provides this region?

options.B: Left horn of the sinus venosus
options.C: Right horn and body of the sinus venosus

questions.explanation: Incorporation of the right sinus horn and body forms the smooth right atrial region.

questions.stem: The left horn of the sinus venosus becomes which adult structure?
questions.explanation: The left sinus horn forms the coronary sinus and is associated with the oblique vein of the left atrium.

questions.stem: The smooth part of the left atrium develops mainly through incorporation of which structure?
questions.explanation: Absorption of pulmonary venous tissue into the atrial wall creates the smooth left atrial region.

questions.stem: As septum primum descends toward the endocardial cushions, what is the initial opening beneath its free edge called?
questions.explanation: Ostium primum initially remains between septum primum and the endocardial cushions.

questions.stem: Before ostium primum closes completely, perforations in the upper septum primum coalesce to form what?
questions.explanation: Formation of ostium secundum maintains interatrial passage as the lower ostium primum closes.

questions.stem: Which structure forms the flap valve of the fetal foramen ovale?
questions.explanation: Septum primum acts as the valve of the foramen ovale and later forms the floor of the fossa ovalis.

questions.stem: After a newborn begins breathing, left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure. Which immediate event normally follows?

options.A: Septum primum is pressed against septum secundum

questions.explanation: The pressure change apposes the two atrial septa, functionally closing the foramen ovale.

questions.stem: Fusion of the superior and inferior endocardial cushions divides which structure?

options.A: The coronary sinus into two arteries
options.B: The common AV canal into right and left AV orifices
options.C: The left ventricle into two atria
options.D: The ductus venosus into pulmonary veins

questions.explanation: AV endocardial cushion fusion divides the common atrioventricular canal.

questions.stem: The membranous interventricular septum forms through fusion involving the muscular septum, conus septum, and which additional structure?
questions.explanation: The lecture attributes the membranous septum to union of the muscular septum, conus septum, and inferior AV cushion.

questions.stem: Neural-crest-derived conotruncal swellings fuse in a spiral course. What is the normal result?

options.A: Fusion of the two atria into one chamber
options.C: Formation of the coronary sinus from the right sinus horn
options.D: Separation of the aortic and pulmonary outflow channels

questions.explanation: The spiral aorticopulmonary septum separates the great arterial outlets.

lecture_sets.subject: Anatomy & Histology
lecture_sets.title: Congenital anomalies of the heart & it’s great Vessels

questions.stem: In the lecture case, Ahmed is 2 years old, becomes cyanotic with feeding or crying, and has a boot-shaped heart. Echocardiography shows VSD, overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, and RV hypertrophy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: These four abnormalities constitute the tetralogy described in the lecture case.

questions.stem: Which developmental change produces the unequal conotruncal division underlying tetralogy of Fallot?

options.A: Failure of the heart tube to fuse at all
options.B: Anterior displacement of the conotruncal septum
options.C: Excessive incorporation of the pulmonary veins
options.D: Early closure of the coronary sinus

questions.explanation: Anterior displacement narrows the pulmonary outlet and produces the characteristic unequal division.

questions.stem: Which finding belongs to the classic tetralogy of Fallot?

options.A: Left ventricular hypertrophy as the defining ventricular change
options.B: Complete absence of an atrial septum

questions.explanation: The four components are pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.stem: A heart tube loops to the left instead of the normal right. Which positional anomaly can result?
questions.explanation: The lecture links leftward cardiac looping to dextrocardia.

questions.stem: Failure of the AV endocardial cushions to fuse produces which defect?

options.B: Transposition caused by a straight conotruncal septum

questions.explanation: Failure of cushion fusion leaves a common AV canal, with atrial and ventricular septal abnormalities.

questions.stem: An infant has an ostium secundum atrial septal defect. Which developmental mechanism is described in the lecture?

options.A: Complete fusion of the semilunar aortic valves
options.B: Excessive resorption of septum primum or inadequate septum secundum development
options.C: Anterior displacement of the conotruncal septum

questions.explanation: These abnormalities leave an excessively large opening in the secundum region of the atrial septum.

questions.stem: An ostium primum atrial septal defect is associated with failure involving which developmental structures?

options.A: The ductus arteriosus and umbilical arteries
options.B: The coronary sinus and left pulmonary vein
options.C: Septum primum and AV endocardial cushions

questions.explanation: The primum defect reflects failure of the lower atrial septum to unite appropriately with the endocardial cushions.

questions.stem: Complete absence of atrial septation produces which anomaly?
questions.explanation: Failure to form an atrial septum leaves a common atrium.

questions.stem: Premature closure of the fetal foramen ovale may cause which chamber changes described in the lecture?

options.A: Enlargement of the right heart with underdevelopment of the left heart
options.B: Isolated enlargement of the left atrium only

questions.explanation: The lecture describes right atrial and ventricular hypertrophy and an undersized left heart after premature closure.

questions.stem: Most ventricular septal defects involve which part of the interventricular septum?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies the membranous region as the usual site, although muscular involvement may also occur.

questions.stem: A newborn has a single arterial trunk overriding both ventricles and an associated VSD. Which embryologic failure best explains this?

options.A: Normal spiral fusion of conotruncal ridges
options.C: Failure of conotruncal ridges to fuse
options.D: Premature obliteration of the umbilical vein

questions.explanation: Failure of conotruncal septation leaves persistent truncus arteriosus with an associated ventricular septal defect.

questions.stem: A newborn has an aorta arising from the right ventricle and a pulmonary trunk arising from the left ventricle. Which developmental error is responsible?

options.A: Failure of the left sinus horn to form a coronary sinus
options.B: Excessive resorption of septum primum alone
options.C: Leftward bending of the entire heart tube only
options.D: Failure of the conotruncal septum to follow a spiral course

questions.explanation: A straight rather than spiral conotruncal septum produces transposition of the great vessels.

questions.stem: Which congenital lesion follows complete fusion of the aortic semilunar valve cusps?
questions.explanation: Partial fusion may cause stenosis; complete fusion produces aortic valvular atresia.

questions.stem: Before birth, which vessel carries oxygenated placental blood toward the fetus?
questions.explanation: Oxygenated placental blood enters through the umbilical vein; the two umbilical arteries return blood to the placenta.

questions.stem: Which fetal channel allows much umbilical venous blood to bypass the liver and reach the IVC?
questions.explanation: The ductus venosus carries much placental venous blood past the hepatic circulation into the inferior vena cava.

questions.stem: High fetal pulmonary vascular resistance directs much pulmonary-trunk blood into the descending aorta through which channel?
questions.explanation: The fetal ductus arteriosus bypasses the high-resistance pulmonary circulation.

questions.stem: The closed umbilical vein normally becomes which structure?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies ligamentum teres as the postnatal remnant of the umbilical vein.

questions.stem: The obliterated ductus venosus normally becomes which structure?
questions.explanation: Ligamentum venosum is the adult remnant of the ductus venosus.

questions.stem: Which adult ligament is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus?
questions.explanation: Postnatal contraction and closure of the ductus arteriosus produce ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.stem: Which parts of the umbilical arteries remain patent after birth?

options.B: Entire arteries continuing as coronary arteries
options.C: Distal parts forming the ductus venosus
options.D: Proximal parts forming the superior vesical arteries

questions.explanation: The distal portions become medial umbilical ligaments; the proximal portions persist as superior vesical arteries.

questions.stem: Which drug in the leukemia/lymphoma treatment lecture disrupts microtubules and arrests cells in metaphase?
questions.explanation: Vincristine is a vinca alkaloid that inhibits microtubule function and mitosis.

questions.stem: Which anticancer drug forms DNA cross-links after metabolic activation?
questions.explanation: The presentation describes cyclophosphamide as an alkylating agent that cross-links DNA.

questions.stem: Doxorubicin exerts anticancer effects through topoisomerase II inhibition and which additional mechanism?
questions.explanation: The lecture describes anthracycline action through topoisomerase II inhibition and free radicals.

questions.stem: A patient has chronic myeloid leukemia driven by BCR–ABL. Which targeted drug mechanism is appropriate in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Imatinib targets BCR–ABL tyrosine kinase in CML.

questions.stem: Rituximab targets which antigen on B cells?
questions.explanation: Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody used in B-cell malignancies.

questions.stem: A patient with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma receives R-CHOP. Which drug does the R designate?
questions.explanation: The lecture lists rituximab plus CHOP for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

questions.stem: Which regimen is listed for Hodgkin lymphoma?
questions.explanation: ABVD contains doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine.

questions.stem: A patient begins AML induction using the lecture's 7+3 regimen. Which drugs are used?
questions.explanation: The lecture lists seven days of cytarabine with three days of an anthracycline for AML induction.

questions.stem: Acute promyelocytic leukemia is treated with differentiation therapy involving which agent?

options.B: Vincristine as the only differentiation agent
options.C: Rituximab as the only differentiation agent
options.D: Imatinib for all cases regardless of mutation

questions.explanation: The presentation lists ATRA and arsenic trioxide for acute promyelocytic leukemia.

questions.stem: Which pair is listed for maintenance therapy in ALL?
questions.explanation: ALL treatment includes a maintenance phase with 6-mercaptopurine and methotrexate in the lecture.

questions.stem: Which route is used for CNS-directed methotrexate therapy in the ALL treatment lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture describes intrathecal therapy for CNS prophylaxis or treatment in ALL.

questions.stem: An ALL patient has a Philadelphia chromosome/BCR–ABL abnormality. Which additional treatment is listed?

options.C: Rituximab solely because every ALL cell expresses CD20
options.D: A tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib

questions.explanation: BCR–ABL-positive ALL can receive targeted tyrosine kinase inhibition alongside its chemotherapy plan.

questions.stem: Which agent may be included with vincristine, a corticosteroid, and an anthracycline during ALL induction?
questions.explanation: The lecture lists an asparaginase-containing ALL induction combination.

questions.stem: Which drug belongs to CHOP alongside cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and prednisolone?
questions.explanation: CHOP combines cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and a corticosteroid.

questions.stem: A lymphoma patient develops cumulative anthracycline toxicity affecting the heart. Which drug in the regimen is implicated?
questions.explanation: Cardiotoxicity is a characteristic anthracycline adverse effect included in the treatment presentation.

questions.stem: A patient receiving vincristine develops peripheral neuropathy. Which property of the drug helps explain this toxicity?

options.A: Selective blockade of CD20 on neurons

questions.explanation: The lecture lists neuropathy with vincristine, whose microtubule effects also disrupt neuronal function.

lecture_sets.subject: Physiology
lecture_sets.title: Respiratory system L1: mechanics of breathing

questions.stem: Which region carries inspired air without participating directly in alveolar gas exchange?
questions.explanation: The conducting zone transports, warms, humidifies and filters air; gas exchange occurs in the respiratory zone.

questions.stem: Why is the volume of the conducting airways called anatomical dead space?

options.B: It is normally filled with pleural fluid
options.D: It contains air that does not directly exchange gases with pulmonary capillary blood

questions.explanation: Anatomical dead space is ventilated conducting-airway volume without alveolar gas exchange; the lecture gives an approximate adult volume of 150 mL.

questions.stem: A patient has impaired mucociliary clearance. Which normal airway function is most directly reduced?

options.C: Removal of inhaled particles trapped in mucus

questions.explanation: Mucus traps inhaled particles and cilia help clear them from the conducting airways. Surfactant secretion and respiratory muscle contraction are separate functions.

questions.stem: During quiet inspiration, which muscle performs most of the work?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is the principal muscle of quiet inspiration. Internal intercostals and abdominal muscles contribute to forced expiration; sternocleidomastoid is an accessory inspiratory muscle.

questions.stem: When the diaphragm contracts during inspiration, what happens first?

options.A: The vertical diameter of the thorax increases
options.B: The vertical diameter of the thorax decreases

questions.explanation: Downward movement of the contracting diaphragm enlarges the thoracic cavity; the resulting pressure reduction draws air inward.

questions.stem: A patient has a phrenic nerve injury. Which respiratory action is directly impaired?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm. Its injury impairs active inspiration through that muscle, rather than directly removing elastic recoil.

questions.stem: What normally produces expiration during quiet breathing?

options.A: Strong contraction of the abdominal wall on every breath
options.B: Active elevation of the ribs by accessory muscles
options.C: Relaxation of inspiratory muscles followed by elastic recoil

questions.explanation: Quiet expiration is passive: inspiratory muscles relax, and recoil reduces thoracic and lung volume. Forced expiration recruits additional muscles.

questions.stem: During forceful expiration, abdominal muscle contraction helps expel air by which mechanism?

options.A: Preventing the ribs from moving downward
options.B: Increasing abdominal pressure and pushing the diaphragm upward
options.C: Lowering abdominal pressure and pulling the diaphragm downward

questions.explanation: Abdominal compression pushes the diaphragm into the thorax, reducing thoracic volume and assisting expiration.

questions.stem: A breathless patient recruits the sternocleidomastoid and scalene muscles. These muscles primarily assist which action?
questions.explanation: Sternocleidomastoid and scalene muscles are accessory inspiratory muscles, recruited when inspiratory demand rises.

questions.stem: What is the respiratory contribution to acid-base balance emphasized in the lecture?

options.A: Direct urinary excretion of hydrogen ions
options.B: Formation of urea in the liver

questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide contributes to carbonic acid formation. Adjusting its elimination helps regulate acid-base balance; renal hydrogen excretion is a different mechanism.

questions.stem: Which process describes cellular respiration as used in the lecture?

options.A: Expansion of the chest wall alone
options.B: Filtering particles in the nasal cavity
options.C: Intracellular use of oxygen to generate energy with carbon dioxide production
options.D: Movement of air through the trachea alone

questions.explanation: Cellular respiration uses oxygen in cellular energy production. Ventilation is the movement of air into and out of the lungs.

questions.stem: During inspiration, external intercostal contraction expands the chest mainly by which action?

options.B: Moving the ribs upward and outward
options.C: Depressing the ribs downward and inward

questions.explanation: External intercostals elevate the ribs and expand the thorax. A larger thoracic volume promotes the pressure gradient for inspiration.

lecture_sets.subject: Physiology
lecture_sets.title: Mechanism of breathing L2: pressures, surfactant and compliance

questions.stem: Which pressure difference is the transpulmonary pressure?

options.D: Pulmonary arterial pressure minus venous pressure

questions.explanation: Transpulmonary pressure is the distending pressure across the lung: alveolar minus intrapleural pressure. A positive value opposes inward lung recoil.

questions.stem: Why is intrapleural pressure normally negative during quiet breathing?

options.A: Alveolar air is continuously removed by cilia
options.B: Pleural fluid is replaced by atmospheric air
options.C: The diaphragm remains maximally contracted throughout expiration
options.D: The lung recoils inward while the chest wall tends outward within a closed pleural space

questions.explanation: Opposing recoil forces in the closed pleural space generate subatmospheric pressure and help keep the lungs expanded.

questions.stem: A chest injury allows air into the pleural space. What directly explains collapse of the affected lung?

options.A: An immediate increase in lung elastic tissue
options.B: A fall in atmospheric pressure outside the body
options.C: Loss of the normal transpulmonary distending pressure
options.D: An immediate increase in surfactant secretion

questions.explanation: Pleural air disrupts the normally negative pleural pressure. Reduced distending pressure allows inward elastic recoil to collapse the lung.

questions.stem: At the start of spontaneous inspiration, which alveolar pressure change draws air inward?

options.A: It becomes identical to systemic arterial pressure
options.D: It remains above atmospheric pressure throughout inspiration

questions.explanation: Thoracic expansion lowers alveolar pressure below atmospheric pressure, creating inward airflow. At the end of inspiration it returns toward atmospheric pressure.

questions.stem: At the end of a normal inspiration, airflow stops despite an expanded lung. Why?

options.A: Alveolar pressure has returned to atmospheric pressure
options.B: Intrapleural pressure has become permanently positive

questions.explanation: Airflow depends on the pressure difference between atmosphere and alveoli. When the difference is zero, flow stops even though lung volume remains above its resting level.

questions.stem: Which expression defines lung compliance?

options.A: Change in distending pressure divided by change in lung volume
options.C: Lung volume divided by respiratory frequency
options.D: Change in lung volume divided by change in distending pressure

questions.explanation: Compliance expresses how much the lung volume changes for a given change in distending pressure. Its inverse describes stiffness or elastance.

questions.stem: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis needs a larger inspiratory pressure change to take the same tidal volume. What has changed?

options.B: Alveolar surface tension has become zero

questions.explanation: Fibrosis stiffens the lung, decreasing compliance. More inspiratory effort is required to achieve a given volume change.

questions.stem: Why can increased compliance in emphysema coexist with difficult expiration?

options.B: The lung expands easily but has lost elastic recoil needed for efficient emptying
options.C: The lung is unusually stiff during inspiration
options.D: All conducting airways become gas-exchanging surfaces

questions.explanation: Destruction of alveolar walls reduces recoil and increases compliance. Easy inflation does not imply effective passive emptying.

questions.stem: Which cells synthesize and secrete pulmonary surfactant?
questions.explanation: Type II alveolar cells produce surfactant, a phospholipid-protein mixture that lowers alveolar surface tension.

questions.stem: A premature infant has surfactant deficiency. Which mechanical consequence is expected?

options.A: Reduced alveolar surface tension and increased compliance
options.C: Complete loss of pulmonary elastic tissue
options.D: Increased alveolar surface tension and reduced lung compliance

questions.explanation: Without adequate surfactant, surface tension rises, alveoli are more prone to collapse and greater effort is needed for inflation.

questions.stem: For two idealized alveoli with equal surface tension, what does Laplace’s law predict about the smaller alveolus?

options.A: Its pressure is independent of radius
options.B: Its pressure must equal pleural pressure
options.C: It requires a higher pressure to remain open
options.D: It requires a lower pressure to remain open

questions.explanation: For an idealized spherical alveolus, P = 2T/r. At equal surface tension, a smaller radius gives a higher pressure; surfactant helps stabilize small alveoli by reducing their tension.

questions.stem: How does surfactant help prevent a small alveolus from emptying into a larger one?

options.B: It lowers surface tension more strongly as its molecules become concentrated in the smaller alveolus
options.C: It raises surface tension most in the smallest alveoli
options.D: It replaces the alveolar air with fluid

questions.explanation: Surfactant molecules become more closely packed as alveoli shrink, lowering surface tension and helping stabilize alveoli of different sizes.

lecture_sets.subject: Pathology
lecture_sets.title: COPD: chronic bronchitis, emphysema and bronchiectasis

questions.stem: Which spirometric relationship supports an obstructive ventilatory defect?

options.A: FEV1 falls proportionately more than FVC, reducing FEV1/FVC
options.C: FEV1 and FVC are always normal
options.D: FVC rises while FEV1 is unchanged in every case

questions.explanation: Airflow obstruction disproportionately reduces forced expiratory volume in the first second, lowering FEV1/FVC. Air trapping can also increase total lung capacity.

questions.stem: A smoker has productive cough for four months in each of two consecutive years. Which clinical definition does this pattern meet, after other causes are excluded?
questions.explanation: Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically by productive cough for at least three months in each of two consecutive years. Emphysema is defined by structural alveolar destruction.

questions.stem: Which bronchial change is characteristic of chronic bronchitis?

options.A: Selective destruction of alveolar septa without airway change
options.C: Enlargement of mucus-secreting glands with an increased Reid index
options.D: Complete replacement of mucous glands by cartilage

questions.explanation: Chronic bronchitis increases the mucus-gland thickness relative to bronchial wall thickness. The lecture describes a Reid index above 50%, versus a normal value below 40%.

questions.stem: What contributes to small-airway narrowing in chronic bronchitis?

options.C: Loss of all airway mucus production

questions.explanation: Goblet-cell hyperplasia and mucus plugs narrow bronchioles, contributing to airflow obstruction.

questions.stem: Which structural change defines emphysema?

options.A: Enlargement of distal airspaces with destruction of alveolar septa
options.C: Fibrotic thickening of every alveolar septum

questions.explanation: Emphysema involves enlarged airspaces and alveolar wall destruction, classically without obvious fibrosis. Loss of recoil contributes to expiratory collapse and air trapping.

questions.stem: A long-term smoker has emphysema predominantly involving respiratory bronchioles in the upper lobes. Which pattern is most likely?
questions.explanation: Centriacinar emphysema preferentially affects central acinar portions and upper lobes and is strongly associated with smoking.

questions.stem: A young patient with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency develops lower-lobe-predominant emphysema. Which distribution is expected within each acinus?

options.A: Involvement only immediately next to a scar
options.B: Sparing of all alveolar ducts and sacs
options.C: Uniform involvement of the whole acinus
options.D: Selective involvement of only the central respiratory bronchiole

questions.explanation: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency classically causes panacinar emphysema, involving the whole acinus and often most severely affecting lower lobes.

questions.stem: How does alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency promote emphysema?

options.A: It increases elastic-fiber synthesis enough to stiffen alveoli
options.B: It leaves alveolar walls insufficiently protected against proteases
options.C: It directly increases bronchial cartilage formation
options.D: It prevents all neutrophils from entering the lung

questions.explanation: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is an antiprotease. Deficiency shifts the protease-antiprotease balance toward tissue destruction.

questions.stem: Which mechanism links cigarette smoke to alveolar wall destruction?

options.A: Inflammation with protease release and oxidant injury
options.C: Permanent elimination of all airway proteases
options.D: Selective increase in intact alveolar elastic tissue

questions.explanation: Smoke-related inflammation releases elastases, oxidants and cytokines. Protease-antiprotease and oxidant-antioxidant imbalances promote alveolar destruction.

questions.stem: Subpleural distal-acinar emphysema is particularly associated with which complication?
questions.explanation: Distal acinar (paraseptal) emphysema affects regions near the pleura and is associated with spontaneous pneumothorax.

questions.stem: Which emphysema pattern is associated with healed inflammatory scars?

options.B: Diffuse alveolar fibrosis without airspace enlargement
options.D: Uniform panacinar emphysema in every lobe

questions.explanation: Irregular emphysema involves the acinus unevenly and is associated with scarring from prior inflammatory disease.

questions.stem: A patient has recurrent lung infections, foul-smelling sputum and permanently dilated bronchi. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis is permanent bronchial dilation following severe inflammatory damage to airway walls; recurrent infection and purulent sputum are typical.

questions.stem: A patient with bronchiectasis also has chronic sinusitis, infertility and situs inversus. Which defect best links these findings?
questions.explanation: Impaired ciliary motility from a dynein-arm defect causes poor airway clearance; the combination with situs inversus is classically Kartagener syndrome.

questions.stem: A child develops recurrent infection and bronchiectasis distal to an aspirated foreign body. What initiated this localized disease?

options.B: A congenital absence of all alveoli
options.D: Airway obstruction followed by infection and wall damage

questions.explanation: A foreign body or tumor can obstruct a localized bronchus, predisposing to infection and destructive inflammation that permanently dilates the airway.

questions.stem: Why does cystic fibrosis predispose to bronchiectasis in the lecture’s disease sequence?

options.B: Lack of pleural fluid directly dilates bronchi
options.C: Abnormal secretions lead to obstruction, infection and airway-wall damage
options.D: Reduced blood pressure destroys bronchial cartilage

questions.explanation: Abnormal exocrine secretions in cystic fibrosis promote airway obstruction and infection, followed by destructive inflammation and bronchiectasis.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced COPD develops pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure. What term describes this cardiac complication?
questions.explanation: Cor pulmonale is right-heart disease resulting from pulmonary disease; the lecture lists pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale among COPD complications.

questions.stem: An instrument damages the main neurovascular bundle in a rib's costal groove. What is its order from superior to inferior?
questions.explanation: The main intercostal bundle lies in the costal groove in VAN order from above downward.

questions.stem: An intercostal nerve is exposed during dissection. Between which muscle layers should it be found?
questions.explanation: The neurovascular plane lies between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles.

questions.stem: After axillary surgery, sensation is reduced over the floor of the axilla and medial upper arm. Which thoracic nerve branch is implicated?
questions.explanation: The lateral cutaneous branch of the second intercostal nerve forms the intercostobrachial nerve supplying these areas.

questions.stem: A groove anterior to the scalene tubercle is identified on the first rib. Which vessel occupies it?
questions.explanation: On the first rib the subclavian vein lies anterior to the scalene tubercle and the artery lies posterior to it.

questions.stem: The head of a typical sixth rib is examined. Which vertebral bodies does it articulate with?
questions.explanation: A typical rib head articulates with its corresponding vertebral body and the body above.

questions.stem: Upward and forward movement of the sternum during inspiration primarily enlarges which diameter?
questions.explanation: Elevation of the sternum increases the anteroposterior diameter; elevation of the rib shafts increases the transverse diameter.

questions.stem: Which ribs attach directly to the sternum through their own costal cartilages?
questions.explanation: The upper seven pairs are true ribs with direct cartilaginous attachments to the sternum.

questions.stem: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the thoracic inlet?
questions.explanation: The inlet is bounded posteriorly by T1, laterally by the first ribs and anteriorly by the superior manubrial border.

questions.stem: What is the fiber direction of external intercostal muscles?
questions.explanation: External intercostal fibers descend forward; internal and innermost fibers descend backward.

questions.stem: Where is the external intercostal muscle replaced by a membrane anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The external muscle extends from the rib tubercle to the costochondral junction, then continues as the external intercostal membrane.

questions.stem: Which vessel gives rise to the internal thoracic artery?

options.C: First part of the subclavian artery

questions.explanation: The internal thoracic artery arises from the first part of the subclavian artery.

questions.stem: The posterior intercostal arteries of the lower nine spaces arise from which vessel?
questions.explanation: The upper two posterior intercostal arteries arise from the superior intercostal artery; the remaining nine arise from the thoracic aorta.

questions.stem: Which nerves continue into the anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The lower intercostal nerves continue into the abdominal wall to supply its muscles, skin and peritoneum.

questions.stem: Deep lymphatics from the anterior thoracic wall primarily drain to which nodes?
questions.explanation: Deep anterior lymph follows the internal thoracic vessels to parasternal nodes; superficial anterior lymph drains to pectoral axillary nodes.

questions.stem: Which joint connects a rib tubercle to its corresponding vertebra?
questions.explanation: The tubercle meets the transverse process at a synovial costotransverse joint; the head meets vertebral bodies at costovertebral joints.

lecture_sets.subject: Anatomy & Histology
lecture_sets.title: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: A patient has obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct at its nasal opening. Which meatus is involved?
questions.explanation: The nasolacrimal duct opens beneath the inferior nasal concha into the inferior meatus.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: Drainage of a sphenoidal sinus infection is obstructed. Which space contains its normal opening?
questions.explanation: The sphenoidal sinus drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: A child has bleeding from the anterior nasal septum. Which vascular area is the likely source?
questions.explanation: Little's area contains Kiesselbach's arterial plexus on the anterior nasal septum.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: Infection spreads from the nose toward the cavernous sinus. Which feature facilitates this spread?

options.B: Direct communication with the middle ear

questions.explanation: Valveless nasal venous connections permit spread toward intracranial veins, including the cavernous sinus.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: A lesion interrupts the greater petrosal nerve. Which nasal function is most directly affected?
questions.explanation: The greater petrosal nerve carries facial parasympathetic fibers to the pterygopalatine ganglion for glandular secretion.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: Which two bones form the main bony nasal septum?

options.B: Perpendicular plate of ethmoid and vomer

questions.explanation: The bony septum contains the ethmoid perpendicular plate superiorly and the vomer inferiorly, with septal cartilage anteriorly.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: Which nasal concha is a separate bone?
questions.explanation: The inferior concha is independent, whereas the superior and middle conchae are parts of the ethmoid.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: The posterior ethmoidal air cells drain into which meatus?
questions.explanation: Posterior ethmoidal cells drain into the superior meatus; anterior and middle groups drain into the middle meatus.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: The maxillary sinus normally drains through which structure?
questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus opens into the hiatus semilunaris in the middle meatus.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: Which artery supplies most of the lateral nasal wall?
questions.explanation: The sphenopalatine artery, a maxillary artery branch, supplies much of the lateral nasal wall.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: Where is olfactory mucosa concentrated?

options.C: Roof and upper parts of the septum and lateral wall
options.D: Floor of the nasal cavity only

questions.explanation: Olfactory receptors occupy the roof and upper nasal walls; most remaining mucosa is respiratory.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the muscles of the external nose?
questions.explanation: These are muscles of facial expression, so their motor supply is facial nerve.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: The pterygopalatine ganglion is functionally associated with which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: Its parasympathetic input comes from the facial nerve via the greater petrosal nerve; it is anatomically associated with V2.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: Which structure forms most of the anterior nasal floor?
questions.explanation: The palatine processes form the anterior three quarters of the nasal floor, and palatine bones form the posterior part.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: What forms the nerve of the pterygoid canal?

options.C: Greater petrosal and deep petrosal nerves

questions.explanation: Parasympathetic greater petrosal and sympathetic deep petrosal fibers unite as the nerve of the pterygoid canal.
questions.concept: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses

questions.stem: After neck surgery, a patient cannot tense the vocal folds effectively. Which muscle is impaired?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid lengthens and tenses the vocal ligaments and is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.

questions.stem: Both vocal folds fail to abduct during inspiration. Which muscle normally produces this movement?
questions.explanation: Posterior cricoarytenoid is the abductor of the vocal folds, opening the glottic airway.

questions.stem: A recurrent laryngeal nerve is injured. Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle retains its usual motor supply?
questions.explanation: All intrinsic muscles receive recurrent laryngeal motor supply except cricothyroid, supplied by the external superior laryngeal branch.

questions.stem: A lesion removes sensation above the vocal folds. Which nerve is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: The internal superior laryngeal branch supplies sensory innervation above the vocal folds.

questions.stem: A surgeon identifies a nerve passing through the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery. Which nerve is it?
questions.explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal vessels.

questions.stem: Which laryngeal cartilage forms a complete ring around the airway?
questions.explanation: The cricoid is a signet-shaped complete ring, with an anterior arch and posterior lamina.

questions.stem: Which paired cartilage provides a vocal process for attachment of the vocal ligament?
questions.explanation: Each arytenoid has an anterior vocal process and a lateral muscular process.

questions.stem: The free inferior border of the quadrangular membrane forms which ligament?
questions.explanation: The inferior border forms the vestibular ligament, covered by mucosa as the false vocal fold.

questions.stem: Where is the laryngeal ventricle located?
questions.explanation: The ventricle is a lateral recess between the false and true vocal folds.

questions.stem: Which muscle adducts the vocal folds by rotating the arytenoid cartilages inward?
questions.explanation: Lateral cricoarytenoid produces adduction, whereas posterior cricoarytenoid abducts the folds.

questions.stem: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is unpaired?
questions.explanation: The transverse arytenoid spans between the arytenoid cartilages and is the unpaired intrinsic muscle.

questions.stem: Sensory innervation below the vocal folds travels in which nerve?
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is sensory below the folds and motor to most intrinsic muscles.
