questions.stem: Which artery gives origin to the superior laryngeal artery?
questions.explanation: The superior laryngeal artery branches from the superior thyroid artery and enters through the thyrohyoid membrane.

questions.stem: Which joint permits thyroid cartilage tilting that increases vocal ligament tension?
questions.explanation: Tilting at the cricothyroid joints increases the distance between vocal ligament attachments and increases tension.

questions.stem: Which muscle widens the laryngeal inlet?
questions.explanation: Thyroepiglottic widens the inlet; aryepiglottic and oblique arytenoid contribute to inlet closure.

questions.stem: A diseased bronchopulmonary segment is removed while neighboring segments are preserved. Which feature permits this?

options.A: Its own segmental bronchus and pulmonary artery branch
options.B: Its own lobar bronchus and lobar artery
options.C: Pulmonary veins running centrally within each segment
options.D: Complete pleural partitions between adjacent segments

questions.explanation: Each segment has its own bronchus and pulmonary arterial branch, making it a surgically separable unit.

questions.stem: During segmental resection, a vessel is found between adjacent segments. Which vessel is expected here?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary veins run intersegmentally, while the bronchus and pulmonary artery run within each segment.

questions.stem: A medial lung surface has a large impression for the left ventricle and grooves for the aortic arch and descending aorta. Which lung is it?
questions.explanation: These are characteristic left lung relations; the right cardiac impression is mainly for the right atrium.

questions.stem: A fissure separates the upper and middle lobes. Which fissure is being observed?
questions.explanation: Only the right lung has a horizontal fissure, separating its superior and middle lobes.

questions.stem: A lesion near the right lung root abuts the arch of a large systemic vein. Which vein is involved?
questions.explanation: The arch of the azygos vein is a characteristic relation of the right lung root and medial surface.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes the left lung from the right?
questions.explanation: The left lung has two lobes, a lingula and a cardiac notch; the right has three lobes.

questions.stem: What supports the concave base of each lung?
questions.explanation: The lung base rests on the diaphragm; its costal surface faces the ribs.

questions.stem: Where is the lung apex relative to the clavicle?

options.B: At the inferior angle of the scapula

questions.explanation: The apex projects about one inch above the medial third of the clavicle into the root of the neck.

questions.stem: At the midaxillary line, the lower border of the lung is approximately at which rib?
questions.explanation: The surface landmarks are ribs 6, 8 and 10 at the midclavicular, midaxillary and posterior regions respectively.

questions.stem: Which structures form the posterior component of the lung hilum?
questions.explanation: The bronchi lie posteriorly at the hilum; the pulmonary veins are more anterior and inferior.

questions.stem: The bronchial arteries primarily supply which structures?
questions.explanation: Bronchial arteries are the systemic nutritive supply to bronchi, lung substance and visceral pleura.

questions.stem: Lymph leaving the bronchopulmonary hilar nodes next passes to which nodes?

options.C: Deep cervical nodes directly, bypassing tracheobronchial nodes

questions.explanation: Lung lymph reaches hilar bronchopulmonary nodes and then tracheobronchial nodes before bronchomediastinal trunks.

questions.stem: Which nerve provides parasympathetic fibers to the pulmonary plexus?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary plexus receives vagal parasympathetic fibers and sympathetic fibers from the sympathetic trunk.

questions.stem: Which right lung lobe contains medial and lateral bronchopulmonary segments?
questions.explanation: The right middle lobe consists of medial and lateral segments; the lingula belongs to the left lung.

questions.stem: Which heart chamber mainly forms the right lung's cardiac impression?
questions.explanation: The medial right lung relates primarily to the right atrium, whereas the left lung has a deeper left ventricular impression.

questions.stem: A small airway has smooth muscle but no cartilage or submucosal glands. Which structure is most likely?
questions.explanation: Absence of both cartilage and glands distinguishes bronchioles from bronchi.

questions.stem: An airway section contains scattered alveoli interrupting a cuboidal epithelial wall. Which structure is it?
questions.explanation: Respiratory bronchioles are the first airways with alveoli in their walls and participate in gas exchange.

questions.stem: A premature infant has alveolar collapse associated with insufficient surfactant. Which cells are functionally deficient?
questions.explanation: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant, lowering surface tension and helping prevent alveolar collapse.

questions.stem: After alveolar epithelial injury, which cells can proliferate and replace type I pneumocytes?
questions.explanation: Type II pneumocytes are surfactant-secreting cells that also regenerate the alveolar epithelium.

questions.stem: An emphysematous lung has destroyed alveolar septa. What functional consequence follows directly?

options.A: Reduced surface area for gas exchange
options.C: Increased diffusion distance from septal thickening

questions.explanation: Destruction of alveolar walls removes exchange surface and associated capillaries.

questions.stem: Which epithelium normally lines most of the trachea?

options.B: Ciliated pseudostratified columnar with goblet cells

questions.explanation: Respiratory epithelium traps particles in mucus and moves them toward the pharynx with cilia.

questions.stem: Which cell forms most of the thin alveolar exchange surface?
questions.explanation: Type I pneumocytes are flattened cells forming the thin barrier for gas diffusion.

questions.stem: Which cell engulfs inhaled particles within alveoli?
questions.explanation: Alveolar macrophages, or dust cells, phagocytose particles and microorganisms in distal airspaces.

questions.stem: Which epithelium covers the true vocal folds?
questions.explanation: The true vocal folds are covered by protective stratified squamous epithelium, unlike most laryngeal mucosa.

questions.stem: Which cartilage arrangement is characteristic of intrapulmonary bronchi?
questions.explanation: Intrapulmonary bronchi have cartilage plates, whereas the trachea has incomplete hyaline rings and bronchioles lack cartilage.

questions.stem: What is the final purely conducting airway?
questions.explanation: Terminal bronchioles end the conducting portion; respiratory bronchioles begin the gas-exchanging portion.

questions.stem: Which cells are characteristic nonciliated secretory cells of terminal bronchioles?
questions.explanation: Club cells produce protective surfactant-like secretions; goblet cells are absent from normal terminal bronchioles.

questions.stem: Which structures form the thin blood-air barrier?

options.A: Type I cell, fused basement membranes and capillary endothelium
options.B: Type II cell, cartilage and capillary endothelium
options.C: Type I cell, smooth muscle and venous endothelium
options.D: Ciliated cell, fused basement membranes and capillary endothelium

questions.explanation: The barrier is minimized by thin type I cells, fused epithelial/endothelial basal laminae and capillary endothelial cells.

questions.stem: What is a consequence of alveolar pores connecting adjacent alveoli?

options.B: Pressure equalization and possible spread of infection
options.C: Active removal of mucus by cilia

questions.explanation: Alveolar pores permit communication and pressure equalization but can also allow infection to spread.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes olfactory mucosa from ordinary respiratory mucosa?

options.C: Bipolar sensory neurons and absence of goblet cells

questions.explanation: Olfactory mucosa contains supporting cells, basal cells and bipolar olfactory neurons, and lacks goblet cells.

questions.stem: A newborn coughs and aspirates during feeding because the trachea communicates with the esophagus. Which developmental event failed?

options.A: Separation of the foregut by the tracheoesophageal septum
options.C: Division of the cardiac outflow tract

questions.explanation: Incomplete separation of ventral respiratory and dorsal esophageal channels produces tracheoesophageal fistula.

questions.stem: A fetus has esophageal atresia and excess amniotic fluid. What explains the excess fluid?
questions.explanation: Esophageal atresia prevents normal swallowing and recycling of amniotic fluid, causing polyhydramnios.

questions.stem: A premature infant has increased alveolar surface tension and repeated collapse. Which missing substance explains this?
questions.explanation: Surfactant lowers surface tension; deficiency makes alveoli collapse and inflation difficult.

questions.stem: A fetal lung shows terminal bronchioles but lacks adequate respiratory units for gas exchange. Which phase fits best?
questions.explanation: The pseudoglandular phase forms conducting branches through terminal bronchioles; respiratory maturation follows.

questions.stem: An infant's lungs continue growing after birth. Which process accounts for much of this growth?
questions.explanation: Postnatal lung growth includes continued alveolar formation as well as enlargement; it is not simply expansion of the alveoli present at birth.

questions.stem: The respiratory diverticulum initially arises from which tissue?
questions.explanation: The lung bud appears as a ventral outpouching of foregut endoderm in the fourth week.

questions.stem: Which embryonic layer gives rise to respiratory epithelial lining?
questions.explanation: The lining of the larynx, trachea, bronchi and lungs is derived from foregut endoderm.

questions.stem: The cartilage and smooth muscle of the trachea and lungs arise mainly from which tissue?
questions.explanation: The surrounding visceral or splanchnic mesoderm forms supporting connective tissue, cartilage and muscle.

questions.stem: Laryngeal muscles and cartilages develop from which pharyngeal arches?
questions.explanation: The fourth and sixth arches contribute laryngeal mesenchyme and explain vagal innervation.

questions.stem: How many secondary bronchial buds normally form on the right and left respectively?
questions.explanation: Secondary bronchi foreshadow the adult lobes: three on the right and two on the left.

questions.stem: Which change characterizes the canalicular period?

options.C: Respiratory bronchioles develop and vascularity increases

questions.explanation: During the canalicular phase distal airways and their blood supply develop toward a functional exchange interface.

questions.stem: Which cells begin secreting pulmonary surfactant during fetal lung maturation?
questions.explanation: Type II cells produce surfactant to reduce tension at the air-liquid interface.

questions.stem: Which mesodermal layer forms visceral pleura?
questions.explanation: Splanchnic mesoderm covering the lung forms visceral pleura; somatic mesoderm lining the body wall forms parietal pleura.

questions.stem: Which process restores the temporarily occluded embryonic laryngeal lumen?
questions.explanation: Proliferating laryngeal epithelium temporarily occludes the lumen, followed by vacuolization and recanalization.

questions.stem: Why can antenatal corticosteroids benefit a fetus at risk of preterm delivery?

options.A: They improve oxygenation by increasing fetal hemoglobin affinity
options.C: They accelerate lung maturation and surfactant synthesis
options.D: They prevent collapse by increasing airway cartilage

questions.explanation: The lecture links antenatal steroids to accelerated maturation and surfactant synthesis, reducing consequences of immaturity.

lecture_sets.subject: Physiology
lecture_sets.title: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: Pulmonary fibrosis doubles diffusion distance while other factors remain unchanged. What happens to gas transfer?
questions.explanation: Fick's law states diffusion rate is inversely related to membrane thickness.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: A patient with emphysema loses alveolar septa. Which diffusion factor is primarily reduced?
questions.explanation: Loss of alveolar walls reduces the available surface area for diffusion.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: During exercise, more pulmonary capillaries are perfused. How does this improve diffusion?
questions.explanation: Recruitment of pulmonary capillaries increases the effective alveolar-capillary area and diffusing capacity.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: Lung disease impairs oxygen transfer more than carbon dioxide transfer. Which gas property helps explain this?

options.B: Carbon dioxide has no molecular weight
options.D: Carbon dioxide is much more soluble

questions.explanation: CO2 has much higher solubility than O2, allowing it to diffuse more readily across the barrier.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: A pulmonary vessel is blocked while its alveoli remain ventilated. What happens to local ventilation/perfusion ratio?

options.D: It becomes independent of blood flow

questions.explanation: Reducing perfusion while ventilation persists raises V/Q and creates wasted ventilation.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: An airway is blocked but its alveoli remain perfused. What happens to local V/Q?

options.A: It rises because perfusion is preserved

questions.explanation: Reduced ventilation with maintained perfusion produces low V/Q and impairs oxygenation.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: Gas movement across the respiratory membrane normally occurs by what mechanism?

options.C: Passive diffusion down partial pressure gradients

questions.explanation: Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse down their respective partial pressure gradients.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: Which change increases diffusion rate if all other factors remain constant?
questions.explanation: A larger driving partial pressure gradient increases gas transfer according to Fick's law.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: What is meant by diffusing capacity?

options.A: Gas volume transferred per minute per unit pressure difference
options.B: Total lung volume after maximal inspiration

questions.explanation: Diffusing capacity describes transfer per minute for each 1 mmHg partial pressure difference.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: Which condition increases respiratory membrane thickness?
questions.explanation: Fluid accumulation between alveoli and capillaries increases diffusion distance in pulmonary edema.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: What do pores of Kohn permit?
questions.explanation: These small interalveolar pores provide collateral airflow between adjacent alveoli.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: Which layers must oxygen cross to enter pulmonary blood?
questions.explanation: The respiratory barrier includes the alveolar lining, basement membranes/interstitium and capillary endothelium.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: What effect does low local alveolar oxygen have on pulmonary arterioles?
questions.explanation: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction redirects blood away from poorly ventilated regions.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: Why is alveolar oxygen pressure lower than that of dry atmospheric air?

options.B: Humidification, mixing with residual gas and continuous oxygen uptake

questions.explanation: Inspired air is humidified and mixed with existing lung gas while oxygen continuously enters pulmonary blood.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: A normal overall V/Q ratio alone does not prove normal gas exchange because what can occur?

options.A: Ventilation is always absent at the apex
options.C: Ventilation and perfusion can both be reduced proportionately

questions.explanation: A ratio may remain similar when both numerator and denominator fall; absolute ventilation and perfusion still matter.
questions.concept: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow

questions.stem: An anemic patient has a normal arterial oxygen partial pressure. Why can oxygen delivery still be reduced?

options.A: Less hemoglobin is available to carry oxygen
options.C: Hemoglobin can no longer bind reversibly
options.D: Normal partial pressure guarantees normal oxygen content

questions.explanation: Most oxygen is carried by hemoglobin; reduced hemoglobin lowers oxygen content even when dissolved oxygen pressure is normal.

questions.stem: A pulse oximeter shows normal saturation in a patient with low hemoglobin concentration. What has the device primarily measured?

options.B: Percentage of hemoglobin binding sites occupied by oxygen

questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry estimates hemoglobin saturation, not hemoglobin concentration or total oxygen delivery.

questions.stem: Blood reaches a tissue with increased metabolic oxygen use. What promotes oxygen diffusion into the tissue?

options.C: A lower tissue oxygen partial pressure
options.D: A higher tissue oxygen partial pressure than blood

questions.explanation: Consumption lowers tissue PO2, maintaining a gradient for diffusion from blood and promoting unloading.

questions.stem: Blood leaving the lungs has lower carbon dioxide and acidity than tissue blood. How does this favor oxygen loading?

options.A: It prevents oxygen binding to heme
options.C: It converts all hemoglobin to myoglobin

questions.explanation: Lower CO2 and acidity favor a leftward shift and higher affinity, supporting pulmonary oxygen loading.

questions.stem: A patient has carbon monoxide exposure. Which oxygen-transport problem is expected?

options.C: Loss of all dissolved plasma oxygen necessarily

questions.explanation: CO occupies hemoglobin and impairs effective oxygen transport; the lecture classifies this as anemic hypoxia.

questions.stem: In which form is most blood oxygen transported?
questions.explanation: About 98.5% is hemoglobin-bound and only a small fraction is physically dissolved.

questions.stem: How many oxygen molecules can one hemoglobin molecule bind?
questions.explanation: Each hemoglobin molecule has four heme iron atoms, each able to bind one oxygen molecule.

questions.stem: What determines measured blood oxygen partial pressure most directly?
questions.explanation: PO2 reflects physically dissolved oxygen rather than the total oxygen bound to hemoglobin.

questions.stem: What shape is the adult oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?
questions.explanation: The adult hemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid, with a plateau at high PO2 and a steeper tissue-range portion.

questions.stem: What is the functional benefit of the upper plateau of the dissociation curve?

options.A: It prevents any tissue oxygen unloading
options.B: Saturation changes relatively little with moderate falls in high PO2
options.C: Hemoglobin releases all oxygen at any lung PO2
options.D: Oxygen transport no longer requires blood flow

questions.explanation: The plateau buffers hemoglobin saturation against moderate decreases in alveolar oxygen pressure.

questions.stem: A left shift of the dissociation curve indicates which change?

options.C: Greater oxygen affinity and less unloading at a given PO2

questions.explanation: A left shift means tighter oxygen binding; loading is favored but tissue unloading is reduced at the same PO2.

questions.stem: Which change favors a leftward shift of the oxygen dissociation curve?
questions.explanation: Lower temperature, lower CO2, lower acidity and lower 2,3-DPG favor increased hemoglobin affinity.

questions.stem: Which statement describes oxygen binding to normal hemoglobin?

options.C: Possible only after iron becomes ferric

questions.explanation: Reversible binding permits oxygen loading in the lungs and release to tissues.

questions.stem: Why do mature red cells not consume their oxygen cargo through oxidative phosphorylation?

options.D: They use oxygen only at night

questions.explanation: Red cells lack mitochondria and obtain energy through anaerobic glycolysis.

questions.stem: What principle is used by a standard pulse oximeter?

options.C: Different light absorption by oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin

questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry uses light absorption at different wavelengths to estimate the fraction of hemoglobin that is oxygenated.

questions.stem: A patient has reduced TLC with proportionate reductions in FEV1 and FVC. Which pattern is expected?
questions.explanation: Restriction reduces lung volumes, while FEV1/FVC is usually preserved or increased rather than markedly reduced.

questions.stem: An older man has progressive dyspnea, dry cough, basal fibrosis and later honeycombing without a known cause. Which diagnosis fits best?
questions.explanation: The pattern of progressive basal/subpleural fibrosis and honeycombing supports idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.stem: A young woman has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, dry cough and noncaseating granulomas. Which disease is most likely?
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis commonly involves hilar nodes and lungs with noncaseating granulomas.

questions.stem: A sarcoidosis patient develops hypercalcemia. Which mechanism explains it?
questions.explanation: Granuloma histiocytes express 1-alpha hydroxylase, producing active vitamin D and increasing calcium availability.

questions.stem: A worker develops interstitial fibrosis after chronic inhalation of fibrogenic dust. Which cell initiates the inflammatory response to particles?
questions.explanation: Macrophages ingest particles and activate inflammatory pathways that stimulate fibroblasts and collagen deposition.

questions.stem: Which mechanical property is reduced in pulmonary fibrosis?

options.C: Elastic recoil pressure at a given volume

questions.explanation: Fibrotic lungs are stiff and poorly compliant, making inflation difficult.

questions.stem: Which mediator from injured pneumocytes is highlighted in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
questions.explanation: TGF-beta promotes fibroblast activity and fibrosis after epithelial injury.

questions.stem: What is the characteristic radiologic and histologic pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
questions.explanation: The fibrosing pattern of IPF is termed usual interstitial pneumonia, or UIP.

questions.stem: Which finding reflects advanced fibrotic remodeling in IPF?
questions.explanation: Advanced fibrosis destroys and remodels distal airspaces, producing a honeycomb appearance.

questions.stem: Which exposure must be considered before labeling fibrosis idiopathic?
questions.explanation: Known causes, including fibrogenic drugs such as amiodarone or bleomycin, must be excluded before diagnosing IPF.

questions.stem: Eggshell calcification of hilar nodes is most associated with which pneumoconiosis in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies eggshell hilar node calcification as particularly characteristic of silicosis.

questions.stem: Which histologic finding is characteristic of sarcoidosis?
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease with noncaseating epithelioid granulomas.

questions.stem: Which lymphocyte response drives sarcoid granuloma formation?
questions.explanation: CD4 helper T cells release cytokines such as IFN-gamma that promote granulomatous inflammation.

questions.stem: Which complication can follow chronic restrictive lung disease?
questions.explanation: Chronic lung disease can raise pulmonary vascular resistance, leading to pulmonary hypertension and right-heart failure.

questions.stem: Which finding can occur within giant cells in sarcoid granulomas?
questions.explanation: Asteroid bodies are stellate inclusions; Schaumann bodies are calcified concretions that may also be present.

lecture_sets.subject: Pharmacology
lecture_sets.title: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: An asthma patient uses a LABA alone and remains at risk from untreated airway inflammation. Which drug class should accompany LABA therapy?
questions.explanation: LABAs are combined with inhaled corticosteroids in asthma because bronchodilation alone does not adequately treat inflammation.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: An inhaled asthma medicine causes oral candidiasis and hoarseness. Which class is responsible?
questions.explanation: Local corticosteroid deposition can cause candidiasis and dysphonia; mouth rinsing and appropriate spacer use reduce local exposure.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: An asthma patient develops tremor, palpitations and hypokalemia after repeated bronchodilator doses. Which class best explains this?
questions.explanation: Beta2 agonist adverse effects include tremor, tachycardia and potassium movement into cells causing hypokalemia.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: Severe allergic asthma with high IgE remains uncontrolled despite inhaled therapy. Which biologic directly targets IgE?
questions.explanation: Omalizumab binds IgE and reduces its interaction with mast-cell and basophil receptors.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: A patient taking theophylline develops seizures and arrhythmia. What property makes this toxicity important?
questions.explanation: Theophylline has a narrow safety margin and important interactions; toxic levels can produce CNS and cardiac effects.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: Which second messenger increases when a beta2 agonist relaxes airway smooth muscle?

options.A: Intracellular calcium as the primary relaxing signal

questions.explanation: Beta2 receptor stimulation activates adenylyl cyclase and increases cAMP, promoting bronchodilation.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: Which drug blocks cysteinyl leukotriene receptors?
questions.explanation: Montelukast and zafirlukast block leukotriene receptors; zileuton inhibits leukotriene synthesis.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: Which drug inhibits 5-lipoxygenase?
questions.explanation: Zileuton blocks 5-lipoxygenase and decreases leukotriene synthesis; hepatotoxicity is an important adverse effect.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: Which mechanism explains ipratropium-induced bronchodilation?
questions.explanation: Ipratropium reduces vagally mediated bronchoconstriction by blocking muscarinic M3 receptors.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: Which drug is a short-acting beta2 agonist?
questions.explanation: Salbutamol is a rapid short-acting bronchodilator; salmeterol is long acting and the others are different classes.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: Why does cromolyn not rapidly reverse an established bronchospasm?

options.C: It stabilizes mast cells rather than directly relaxing airway muscle
options.D: It is a strong beta2 antagonist

questions.explanation: Cromolyn prevents mediator release and is prophylactic; it is not a direct rescue bronchodilator.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: What is the principal benefit of inhaled corticosteroids in asthma?

options.A: Immediate direct relaxation of all airway muscle
options.D: Suppression of airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness

questions.explanation: Corticosteroids reduce inflammatory mediators and cellular infiltration, controlling the inflammatory component of asthma.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: Which route delivers a smaller drug dose directly to airways with fewer systemic effects?
questions.explanation: Inhaled delivery targets the airways and generally reduces systemic exposure compared with larger systemic doses.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: Which drug can worsen asthma through nonselective beta-receptor blockade?
questions.explanation: Propranolol blocks beta2 receptors and may provoke bronchoconstriction.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: What major immediate hypersensitivity risk is highlighted for omalizumab?
questions.explanation: The lecture highlights anaphylaxis as an important potential adverse effect of anti-IgE therapy.
questions.concept: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

lecture_sets.subject: Pharmacology
lecture_sets.title: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: A COPD patient remains breathless on one long-acting bronchodilator. Why can combining LABA with LAMA improve bronchodilation?

options.A: They act through complementary beta2 and M3 pathways
options.D: They eliminate the need for any inhaler technique

questions.explanation: LABA increases cAMP through beta2 stimulation; LAMA reduces cholinergic constriction through M3 blockade.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: A COPD patient has recurrent exacerbations despite long-acting bronchodilation and high blood eosinophils. Which addition may provide benefit?

options.D: Antibiotic for every day in every patient

questions.explanation: ICS benefit is more likely in selected exacerbation-prone patients with higher eosinophils; it is not routine COPD monotherapy.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: A patient using tiotropium develops dry mouth and urinary retention. Which mechanism explains these effects?
questions.explanation: LAMA antimuscarinic effects can cause dry mouth, urinary retention and ocular symptoms with eye exposure.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: A chronic bronchitis patient with severe airflow limitation and recurrent exacerbations receives roflumilast. What is its target?
questions.explanation: Roflumilast inhibits PDE4, reducing cAMP breakdown and exerting anti-inflammatory effects in selected COPD patients.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: A patient with COPD develops acute worsening of dyspnea. Which inhaled drugs provide short-acting bronchodilation?
questions.explanation: The lecture lists short-acting beta2 agonists with or without short-acting muscarinic antagonists for acute symptom relief.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: What is the foundation of pharmacologic COPD symptom treatment?
questions.explanation: Bronchodilators reduce airflow limitation and symptoms; long-acting agents form maintenance treatment.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: Which agent is a LAMA?
questions.explanation: Tiotropium is long acting; ipratropium is a SAMA and salbutamol is a SABA.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: Which ICS-associated infection risk is particularly relevant in COPD?
questions.explanation: The lecture lists increased pneumonia risk among adverse effects of inhaled corticosteroids in COPD.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: Which adverse effect is characteristic of roflumilast?
questions.explanation: Roflumilast may cause gastrointestinal symptoms, decreased appetite and weight loss.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of ensifentrine?
questions.explanation: PDE3 inhibition contributes bronchodilation and PDE4 inhibition contributes anti-inflammatory activity.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: Which statement describes ensifentrine's role in the lecture?

options.B: Replacement for oxygen in every patient
options.D: First and only emergency rescue therapy

questions.explanation: Ensifentrine is presented as a newer maintenance add-on, not a rescue bronchodilator.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: Why is theophylline's routine role in COPD limited?

options.D: Narrow therapeutic index and significant interactions

questions.explanation: Toxicity, including arrhythmias and seizures, and interactions limit its use when effective inhaled agents are available.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: Which preventive treatment can cause QT prolongation and hearing impairment?
questions.explanation: Long-term azithromycin may help selected frequent exacerbators but carries resistance, QT and hearing risks.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: Which intervention addresses the most important modifiable exposure in smoking-related COPD?

options.A: Increasing inhaler dose without checking technique

questions.explanation: Smoking cessation reduces continued smoke exposure; rehabilitation and inhaler technique also support treatment.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

questions.stem: Which patients are candidates for long-term oxygen in the lecture?

options.B: Only those with isolated nasal congestion
options.C: Appropriately selected patients with severe chronic hypoxemia

questions.explanation: Long-term oxygen is targeted to severe chronic hypoxemia rather than prescribed solely for the COPD label.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1

lecture_sets.subject: Pharmacology
lecture_sets.title: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: A patient has thick tenacious sputum. Which drug directly breaks disulfide bonds in mucus proteins?
questions.explanation: N-acetylcysteine breaks mucoprotein disulfide bonds, reducing viscosity and facilitating clearance.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: A patient taking an MAO inhibitor requests an antitussive. Which drug has an important serotonergic interaction?
questions.explanation: Dextromethorphan has serotonergic interactions and should not be combined with MAO inhibitors.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: A patient chews a benzonatate capsule and develops mouth and pharyngeal numbness. What explains this?

options.C: Local anesthetic effects on sensory receptors

questions.explanation: Benzonatate suppresses peripheral cough receptors and can numb oral/pharyngeal tissues if chewed; capsules are swallowed whole.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: A patient has a productive cough that helps clear secretions. Why should unnecessary suppression be avoided?

options.A: Productive cough never has an underlying cause
options.B: All mucus must remain in the airway
options.D: Cough is a protective clearance reflex

questions.explanation: Suppressing useful productive cough may impede secretion clearance; management should address the cause and aid clearance.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: A patient develops cough after starting an ACE inhibitor. What is the first principle of management?

options.A: Identify and address the underlying cause
options.C: Treat all cough as bacterial pneumonia
options.D: Use a mucolytic regardless of sputum

questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes cause-directed treatment before simply suppressing symptoms.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: Which drug is an opioid central antitussive?
questions.explanation: Codeine suppresses the cough reflex centrally through opioid effects.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: Which adverse-effect combination is characteristic of codeine?
questions.explanation: Codeine's opioid effects include sedation, constipation, dependence and respiratory depression.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: Which drug is classified as an expectorant?
questions.explanation: Guaifenesin facilitates removal of secretions by improving hydration and expectoration.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: How does an expectorant differ from a central antitussive?

options.A: It facilitates secretion clearance rather than suppressing the cough center
options.B: It blocks all mucus production permanently
options.C: It acts as an opioid in the medulla

questions.explanation: Expectorants aid sputum clearance; central antitussives reduce the cough reflex.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: Which agent acts on peripheral cough receptors?
questions.explanation: Benzonatate is the peripheral antitussive in the lecture, unlike central codeine and dextromethorphan.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: Besides its mucolytic role, N-acetylcysteine is an antidote for which toxicity?
questions.explanation: NAC also serves as the antidote for acetaminophen poisoning, as highlighted in the lecture.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: Which adverse effect can occur with inhaled N-acetylcysteine?
questions.explanation: Inhaled NAC can provoke bronchospasm; oral use may cause gastrointestinal upset and an unpleasant taste.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: Which type of cough is the usual target for short-term antitussive therapy when appropriate?

options.B: Every productive cough regardless of cause
options.D: All cough in respiratory failure without assessment

questions.explanation: Antitussives may help troublesome dry cough after assessing the cause and safety; productive cough needs clearance considerations.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: Which pair consists of mucolytics?
questions.explanation: NAC and carbocisteine reduce mucus viscosity; the other pairs belong to different therapeutic classes.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: Which adverse effects are listed for guaifenesin?

options.B: Severe marrow suppression as its usual effect

questions.explanation: Guaifenesin's listed adverse effects are gastrointestinal upset, dizziness and headache.
questions.concept: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2

questions.stem: A CAP regimen combines amoxicillin with clavulanate. What is clavulanate's main contribution?
questions.explanation: Clavulanate protects the beta-lactam from susceptible beta-lactamases rather than acting as the main antibacterial component.

questions.stem: A pneumonia patient needs coverage for atypical organisms in addition to a beta-lactam. Which listed drug supplies this coverage?
questions.explanation: Azithromycin covers atypical organisms such as Mycoplasma and Legionella, which are not reliably covered by these beta-lactams.

questions.stem: A patient takes doxycycline with an iron supplement. What interaction may reduce efficacy?

options.A: Immediate renal destruction of the drug

questions.explanation: Iron and other polyvalent cations interfere with doxycycline absorption; timing and coadministered products matter.

questions.stem: A patient develops tendon pain during treatment with levofloxacin. Which drug class is implicated?
questions.explanation: Tendinitis is an important fluoroquinolone adverse effect highlighted in the lecture.

questions.stem: A patient with renal impairment receives amoxicillin. Why may the regimen need adjustment?

options.B: The drug is eliminated only through the lungs

questions.explanation: Amoxicillin is mainly renally eliminated, so renal impairment can prolong exposure.

questions.stem: What is the principal antibacterial mechanism of beta-lactams?

options.B: PBP binding and inhibition of peptidoglycan cross-linking

questions.explanation: Beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins and inhibit transpeptidation, weakening the bacterial wall.

questions.stem: Which mechanism can inactivate a beta-lactam antibiotic?
questions.explanation: Beta-lactamases hydrolyze the ring, causing loss of antibacterial activity.

questions.stem: Which bacterial target is inhibited by azithromycin?
questions.explanation: Macrolides inhibit protein synthesis through binding to the bacterial 50S subunit.

questions.stem: Which target is inhibited by doxycycline?
questions.explanation: Doxycycline prevents aminoacyl-tRNA association at the 30S ribosome, inhibiting protein synthesis.

questions.stem: How does levofloxacin inhibit bacterial replication?
questions.explanation: Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA-processing enzymes needed for replication.

questions.stem: Which cephalosporin is third generation in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone is third generation; cefuroxime is second generation.

questions.stem: Which patient factor should influence empiric CAP antibiotic selection?
questions.explanation: Comorbidity affects likely pathogens, and recent antibiotics can increase resistant-organism risk.

questions.stem: Why should local resistance data be considered before macrolide monotherapy?

options.A: High resistance can make empiric coverage unreliable
options.D: All CAP is caused by one susceptible organism

questions.explanation: Empiric therapy must account for local susceptibility rather than assume all pneumococci are macrolide-sensitive.

questions.stem: Which feature of levofloxacin supports an oral route when otherwise appropriate?
questions.explanation: Levofloxacin's high oral bioavailability can yield exposure comparable to IV dosing in suitable patients.

questions.stem: What does CURB-65 primarily help assess in CAP?

options.C: Severity and need for higher-level care

questions.explanation: CURB-65 uses clinical and laboratory severity markers to support care-setting decisions, not organism identification.

questions.stem: A patient on isoniazid develops tingling in the feet. Which supplement targets the mechanism of this adverse effect?
questions.explanation: Isoniazid-associated peripheral neuropathy is linked to vitamin B6 deficiency; pyridoxine is used to prevent it.

questions.stem: A patient on TB therapy develops reduced visual acuity and impaired color discrimination. Which drug is most implicated?
questions.explanation: Ethambutol can cause optic neuritis with visual acuity and color-vision changes.

questions.stem: A TB patient notices orange-red urine and tears. Which drug commonly explains this?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin causes characteristic orange-red discoloration of body fluids.

questions.stem: A patient develops hyperuricemia during the intensive phase of TB treatment. Which drug is the classic cause?
questions.explanation: Pyrazinamide is associated with hyperuricemia and may precipitate gout; hepatotoxicity is another key toxicity.

questions.stem: Warfarin effect decreases after rifampicin is started. What mechanism explains this?

options.D: Blocking warfarin absorption by calcium chelation

questions.explanation: Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer and can lower exposure to interacting medicines.

questions.stem: Why are several drugs combined when treating active TB?

options.A: Because each drug is inactive on its own
options.B: To suppress selection of resistant mutants
options.C: To ensure all drugs have identical targets
options.D: To avoid any need for adherence

questions.explanation: Combination therapy attacks different bacterial populations and reduces survival of mutants resistant to a single agent.

questions.stem: What is isoniazid's main cell-wall target?
questions.explanation: Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis after activation within the organism.

questions.stem: Which enzyme activates isoniazid?
questions.explanation: Isoniazid is a prodrug activated by mycobacterial KatG; mutations can produce resistance.

questions.stem: Which target is inhibited by rifampicin?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase; rpoB mutations are a major resistance mechanism.

questions.stem: Which cell-wall enzyme is targeted by ethambutol?
questions.explanation: Ethambutol interferes with arabinogalactan cell-wall synthesis through arabinosyl transferase inhibition.

questions.stem: Resistance to both which drugs defines multidrug-resistant TB?
questions.explanation: MDR-TB is defined by resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin.

questions.stem: Which listed antituberculous aminoglycoside classically causes ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity?
questions.explanation: Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside with important auditory/vestibular and renal toxicities.
questions.review_note: Streptomycin is not a routine component of current first-line HRZE therapy.

questions.stem: Which newer anti-TB drug inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase?
questions.explanation: Bedaquiline disrupts mycobacterial energy generation by inhibiting ATP synthase.

questions.stem: Which adverse effects are particularly important with prolonged linezolid use?
questions.explanation: Linezolid can cause marrow suppression and peripheral or optic neuropathy, especially with prolonged exposure.

questions.stem: Why does irregular TB treatment increase treatment failure and resistance?

options.C: It permits survival and selection of resistant bacterial populations
options.D: It makes every organism more drug-sensitive

questions.explanation: Missed or inconsistent doses weaken effective combination exposure and can select resistant organisms.

questions.stem: A postoperative mucus plug blocks a bronchus and the distal lung collapses. Which type of atelectasis is this?
questions.explanation: Air trapped distal to an obstruction is absorbed without replacement, causing resorption collapse.

questions.stem: A large pleural effusion compresses adjacent lung. Which type of atelectasis results?
questions.explanation: Pleural fluid exerts external pressure on the lung, causing compression atelectasis.

questions.stem: A lung remains poorly expanded after mucus and pleural fluid are removed because of extensive scarring. Which mechanism explains this?
questions.explanation: Fibrosis physically restricts expansion; contraction atelectasis is generally not readily reversible.

questions.stem: A patient with sepsis develops acute hypoxemia, bilateral opacities and edema without cardiac failure. Which injury pattern is expected?
questions.explanation: ARDS involves inflammatory alveolar-capillary injury with noncardiogenic edema and diffuse alveolar damage.

questions.stem: An ARDS biopsy shows pink hyaline membranes lining alveolar ducts. What are they composed of?

options.A: Fibrin-rich edema fluid and necrotic epithelial debris

questions.explanation: Hyaline membranes are formed from leaked protein-rich fluid and damaged epithelial remnants.

questions.stem: Why does atelectasis cause hypoxemia despite continued blood flow?

options.B: Perfusion persists through poorly ventilated lung
options.C: All pulmonary vessels are necessarily thrombosed

questions.explanation: Blood traversing unventilated or poorly ventilated units produces low V/Q and shunt-like gas exchange impairment.

questions.stem: Which factor promotes dependent basal collapse after surgery?
questions.explanation: Shallow breathing fails to recruit dependent alveoli and favors underexpansion.

questions.stem: Which inflammatory cell is central to early ARDS injury?
questions.explanation: Activated neutrophils release reactive oxygen species and proteases that damage the alveolar-capillary barrier.

questions.stem: Which property of the pulmonary vasculature increases in ARDS?
questions.explanation: Endothelial and epithelial injury increases permeability, producing protein-rich pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: What effect does surfactant loss have during ARDS?

options.B: It stiffens alveolar units and favors collapse

questions.explanation: Surfactant loss increases surface tension and contributes to stiff, unstable alveoli.

questions.stem: Which cells proliferate during the organizing stage of diffuse alveolar damage?
questions.explanation: Type II pneumocytes proliferate to repair and regenerate the alveolar lining.

questions.stem: Which process can limit recovery after ARDS?

options.D: Organization of exudate into interstitial fibrosis

questions.explanation: Organization of fibrin-rich exudate can produce fibrosis and septal thickening, impairing lung function.

questions.stem: Which is a recognized systemic trigger of ARDS?
questions.explanation: Pancreatitis can generate systemic inflammation leading to diffuse alveolar injury, alongside triggers such as sepsis and trauma.

questions.stem: Which gross appearance is typical of acute ARDS lungs?

options.B: Heavy, firm, dark red and airless
options.D: Normal weight with isolated cartilage nodules

questions.explanation: Edema, congestion and diffuse injury make the lungs heavy, congested and poorly aerated.

questions.stem: Why should reversible atelectasis be corrected promptly?

options.C: To reduce hypoxemia and retained-secretion infection

questions.explanation: Poor ventilation causes oxygenation impairment and secretion retention, increasing infection risk.

questions.stem: A patient develops pulmonary embolism after prolonged immobilization. Where did the embolus most likely originate?
questions.explanation: Most pulmonary thromboemboli originate in large deep leg veins and travel through the right heart.

questions.stem: A large saddle embolus obstructs major pulmonary arteries and causes shock. Which chamber acutely fails?

options.D: Left ventricle from direct coronary occlusion

questions.explanation: A sudden rise in pulmonary resistance can overwhelm the right ventricle and cause acute cor pulmonale and collapse.

questions.stem: Repeated small emboli progressively reduce the functional pulmonary vascular bed. What complication may develop?

options.A: Isolated systemic hypotension without pulmonary effects

questions.explanation: Chronic obstruction reduces vascular area and increases pulmonary resistance, causing thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A patient with longstanding mitral stenosis develops pulmonary hypertension. What initiates the pressure increase?

options.D: Elevated left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure

questions.explanation: Left-sided valvular disease elevates left atrial pressure, transmitting pressure backward through pulmonary veins.

questions.stem: A lung specimen after embolism contains a peripheral wedge-shaped dark-red lesion. What is it?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary infarcts are characteristically hemorrhagic and wedge shaped, often in lower lobes.

questions.stem: Which inherited signaling abnormality is associated with familial pulmonary arterial hypertension?
questions.explanation: Defective BMPR2 signaling contributes endothelial dysfunction and vascular smooth-muscle proliferation.

questions.stem: Which vascular change characterizes advanced pulmonary arterial hypertension?

options.A: Normal intima with only airway mucus

questions.explanation: Plexiform lesions are complex endothelial proliferations with multiple channels in small pulmonary arteries.

questions.stem: How can COPD lead to pulmonary hypertension?

options.A: Direct obstruction of the aortic valve
options.D: Loss of alveolar capillary bed and increased resistance

questions.explanation: Chronic lung disease can destroy or obliterate capillaries, reducing the vascular bed and raising resistance.

questions.stem: Which cardiac adaptation follows chronic pulmonary hypertension?
questions.explanation: The right ventricle hypertrophies in response to chronically elevated pulmonary afterload and may eventually fail.

questions.stem: Pulmonary hypertension caused by chronic thromboembolism belongs to which group in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Group 4 is chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension; groups 2 and 3 reflect left-heart and lung/hypoxia causes.

questions.stem: Which pulmonary emboli are most likely to be clinically silent?

options.A: Emboli obstructing most of the pulmonary circulation

questions.explanation: Clinical consequences depend strongly on size and vascular obstruction; many small emboli cause few symptoms.

questions.stem: Which factor increases venous thromboembolism risk?

options.C: Low estrogen exposure as an isolated protective setting

questions.explanation: Orthopedic surgery and subsequent immobility increase venous thrombosis risk, creating a potential pulmonary embolic source.

questions.stem: What do lines of Zahn indicate in a pulmonary thrombus?

options.A: Alternating layers of platelets/fibrin and red cells

questions.explanation: Lamination reflects blood flow during thrombus formation, producing pale platelet-fibrin and darker red-cell layers.

questions.stem: Which structural change narrows muscular pulmonary arteries in hypertension?

options.A: Complete disappearance of endothelial cells without remodeling
options.C: Loss of the entire media with uniform dilation

questions.explanation: Myointimal proliferation and smooth-muscle hypertrophy narrow pulmonary arterial lumina and reinforce elevated resistance.

questions.stem: Which symptoms are typical of pulmonary hypertension?

options.A: Painless jaundice as the sole defining feature

questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes dyspnea and fatigue, with possible anginal discomfort and later right-heart consequences.

questions.stem: A patient has consolidation of an entire lung lobe with alveolar neutrophils, red cells and fibrin. Which stage is present?
questions.explanation: Red hepatization produces liver-like consolidation with red cells, neutrophils and fibrin filling alveoli.

questions.stem: A pneumonia specimen is dry, gray and firm with lysed red cells and persistent fibrin. Which stage is this?
questions.explanation: Gray hepatization follows breakdown of red cells while fibrinopurulent exudate remains.

questions.stem: An unconscious patient aspirates infected oral material and develops foul sputum and a cavity with an air-fluid level. What lesion is most likely?
questions.explanation: Aspiration can cause suppurative parenchymal necrosis, forming a pus-containing cavity with an air-fluid level.

questions.stem: A transplant patient has enlarged pulmonary cells with prominent owl's-eye nuclear inclusions. Which infection is implicated?
questions.explanation: CMV produces enlarged cells with characteristic nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions in immunocompromised hosts.

questions.stem: An AIDS patient has dyspnea and foamy intra-alveolar exudate containing silver-staining cup-shaped cysts. Which organism fits?
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis causes foamy alveolar exudate, and silver stains highlight its cysts.

questions.stem: How does bronchopneumonia differ anatomically from lobar pneumonia?

options.B: Patchy consolidation rather than a large continuous lobar area
options.C: Only pleural fluid with no lung involvement

questions.explanation: Bronchopneumonia has patchy consolidation, whereas lobar pneumonia affects much or all of a lobe.

questions.stem: What does pulmonary consolidation represent in acute bacterial pneumonia?

options.B: Accumulation of air only in the pleural space
options.C: Replacement of alveolar air by exudate

questions.explanation: Exudate fills normally air-containing spaces, making lung tissue solid.
questions.review_note: Consolidation has causes other than exudate; specify bacterial pneumonia.

questions.stem: Which organism is highlighted as a common cause of acute community-acquired bacterial pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Pneumococcus is a leading cause of acute bacterial CAP in the lecture.

questions.stem: Which consequence represents spread of pneumonia into the pleural space as pus?
questions.explanation: Empyema is purulent infection of the pleural space, distinct from emphysema of lung parenchyma.

questions.stem: Where is inflammation mainly located in typical atypical interstitial pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Atypical pneumonia features interstitial septal inflammation with mononuclear cells rather than abundant alveolar purulent exudate.

questions.stem: Which organisms are important in hospital-acquired pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Nosocomial pneumonia often involves gram-negative bacilli, including Pseudomonas, and S. aureus.

questions.stem: Which finding favors Actinomyces infection?

options.A: Encapsulated budding yeast with a halo
options.D: Anaerobic branching bacteria with sulfur granules

questions.explanation: Actinomyces are anaerobic filamentous bacteria; sulfur granules are a characteristic tissue finding.

questions.stem: Which feature helps distinguish Nocardia from Actinomyces?

options.D: Ability to cause pulmonary infection alone

questions.explanation: Nocardia is weakly acid fast on modified stains, unlike Actinomyces; both can be branching gram-positive organisms.

questions.stem: Which fungal morphology supports Aspergillus infection?
questions.explanation: Aspergillus typically forms septate hyphae with acute-angle branching in tissue.

questions.stem: How does smoking predispose to pulmonary infection?

options.C: Impaired mucociliary clearance and macrophage activity

questions.explanation: Smoking compromises physical clearance and alveolar immune defenses, increasing infection susceptibility.

questions.stem: A long-term smoker develops persistent hoarseness and a true vocal-cord mass. Which histologic type is most likely?
questions.explanation: Most laryngeal malignancies are squamous cell carcinomas, strongly associated with tobacco exposure.

questions.stem: A small glottic cancer is detected early because it changes the voice. What additional feature favors its prognosis?
questions.explanation: Early hoarseness and limited true-cord lymphatics support earlier diagnosis and less early nodal spread.

questions.stem: A supraglottic carcinoma presents with cervical nodal metastases. Which anatomical feature contributes?

options.A: Direct drainage only to inguinal nodes
options.D: Absence of lymphatics throughout the larynx

questions.explanation: Supraglottic lymphatic richness promotes earlier nodal spread compared with glottic lesions.

questions.stem: An adult has unilateral middle-ear effusion and a nasopharyngeal mass. What explains the ear finding?

options.A: Direct destruction of all cochlear hair cells
options.B: Excess surfactant in the middle ear

questions.explanation: A nasopharyngeal tumor can obstruct the Eustachian tube, impairing middle-ear ventilation and causing effusion.

questions.stem: A nasopharyngeal biopsy shows large undifferentiated epithelial cells in a dense lymphoid background and EBER positivity. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The lymphoepithelioma pattern of NPC has malignant epithelial cells with reactive lymphocytes and a strong EBV association.

questions.stem: Which two exposures have synergistic effects on laryngeal carcinoma risk?
questions.explanation: Alcohol and tobacco together increase laryngeal carcinoma risk more strongly than either exposure alone.

questions.stem: Which virus is strongly associated with endemic nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
questions.explanation: EBV is strongly associated with nonkeratinizing NPC and can be demonstrated with EBER in-situ hybridization.

questions.stem: What is a common first presentation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
questions.explanation: NPC may remain locally occult while early lymphatic spread produces a neck mass.

questions.stem: Which region has a high incidence of endemic nasopharyngeal carcinoma?

options.C: All regions at an identical rate

questions.explanation: The lecture highlights Southern China, Southeast Asia and North Africa in NPC epidemiology.

questions.stem: Which histologic features indicate squamous differentiation in a laryngeal tumor?
questions.explanation: Keratinization and intercellular bridges identify squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: What distinguishes carcinoma in situ from invasive carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Carcinoma in situ can have marked cytologic atypia but has not breached the epithelial basement membrane.

questions.stem: The lymphocytes in lymphoepithelioma-like NPC are principally what?
questions.explanation: The tumor is epithelial; its prominent lymphoid background is reactive and may obscure the malignant cells.

questions.stem: Which technique can demonstrate EBV within tumor nuclei?
questions.explanation: EBER in-situ hybridization detects EBV-encoded RNA and supports EBV-associated NPC.

questions.stem: Why can patients with laryngeal carcinoma develop second upper-aerodigestive primaries?

options.A: Every second lesion is necessarily a metastasis
options.C: All neighboring tissue is protected from carcinogens
options.D: The original tumor must always spread by direct implantation

questions.explanation: Shared tobacco/alcohol exposure produces field injury across mucosa, allowing independent primary tumors.

questions.stem: Which NPC subtype is especially radiosensitive in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The undifferentiated nonkeratinizing subtype is radiosensitive, contributing to the central role of radiotherapy.

questions.stem: A peripheral lung tumor forms malignant glands and produces mucin. Which type is most likely?
questions.explanation: Gland formation and mucin production support adenocarcinoma, which often arises peripherally.

questions.stem: A central lung mass in a smoker shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Central location, smoking and squamous differentiation are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: A central lung tumor contains small cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding and many mitoses. Which type fits?
questions.explanation: Small cell carcinoma is a high-grade neuroendocrine tumor with nuclear molding, scant cytoplasm and high proliferative activity.

questions.stem: A lung cancer patient has hypercalcemia caused by PTH-related peptide. Which tumor association is strongest?
questions.explanation: Squamous lung carcinomas can secrete PTHrP, producing paraneoplastic hypercalcemia.

questions.stem: A patient with an apical lung mass has shoulder pain, ptosis, miosis and facial anhidrosis. Which structure explains the autonomic findings?
questions.explanation: Apical tumors can invade sympathetic pathways, causing Horner syndrome; brachial plexus involvement causes arm pain.

questions.stem: A former shipyard worker develops diffuse malignant pleural disease decades after exposure. Which tumor is most associated?
questions.explanation: Asbestos exposure with long latency is strongly associated with malignant pleural mesothelioma.

questions.stem: Which lung carcinoma is most common overall, including among never-smokers?

options.B: Squamous cell carcinoma in every population

questions.explanation: The lecture identifies adenocarcinoma as the most common primary lung carcinoma and the commonest in never-smokers.

questions.stem: Which molecular result can guide targeted treatment of lung adenocarcinoma?
questions.explanation: Actionable tumor mutations such as EGFR and ALK alterations can guide targeted therapy.

questions.stem: Which tumor is strongly associated with ectopic ADH and ACTH production?
questions.explanation: Small cell carcinoma can cause SIADH and Cushing syndrome through ectopic hormone secretion.

questions.stem: What defines lepidic growth in lung adenocarcinoma?

options.B: Tumor cells growing along preexisting alveolar walls
options.D: Cartilage and fat in a circumscribed nodule

questions.explanation: Lepidic growth follows existing alveolar septa rather than forming a new complex glandular architecture.

questions.stem: Which finding is characteristic of a pulmonary hamartoma?

options.C: A well-circumscribed mixture including cartilage and fat
options.D: High-grade small cells with nuclear molding

questions.explanation: Hamartomas are benign nodules containing disorganized mature tissues such as cartilage, fat and fibrous tissue.

questions.stem: How does typical carcinoid differ from small cell carcinoma?

options.A: Higher grade with obligatory extensive necrosis
options.C: It is always a pleural tumor
options.D: Lower mitotic activity and absence of necrosis

questions.explanation: Typical carcinoids are well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors with low mitoses and no necrosis, unlike high-grade small cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of superior vena cava syndrome in lung malignancy?

options.A: Obstruction of venous return from the head, neck and arms
options.B: Blockage of the inferior vena cava only
options.C: Acute closure of the mitral valve

questions.explanation: Tumor compression or invasion of the SVC causes upper-body venous congestion and swelling.

questions.stem: Loss of which tumor-suppressor pair is characteristic of small cell carcinoma?
questions.explanation: TP53 and RB1 loss are characteristic molecular abnormalities in small cell lung carcinoma.

questions.stem: Which feature supports large cell carcinoma after adequate exclusion of other types?

options.A: Uniform small cells with low mitoses and no necrosis
options.C: Poorly differentiated large malignant cells without definite glandular or squamous differentiation

questions.explanation: Large cell carcinoma is a poorly differentiated NSCLC lacking more specific differentiation after adequate sampling.

questions.stem: A pneumonia outbreak is linked to contaminated building water aerosols. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Legionella is transmitted through contaminated aerosols and can cause building-associated outbreaks.

questions.stem: A patient develops pneumonia after close contact with parrots and pigeons. Which agent is suggested?
questions.explanation: Bird exposure is the epidemiologic clue for psittacosis due to C. psittaci.

questions.stem: A young infant develops bronchiolitis during winter. Which virus is classically implicated?
questions.explanation: RSV is an important cause of lower-airway disease and bronchiolitis in infants.

questions.stem: A child develops repeated coughing bouts followed by an inspiratory whoop. Which organism causes this syndrome?
questions.explanation: B. pertussis causes a catarrhal illness followed by paroxysmal coughing and the characteristic inspiratory whoop.

questions.stem: A patient with weight loss, night sweats and chronic cough has an apical cavitating lesion. Which stain can demonstrate the suspected bacilli?
questions.explanation: Ziehl–Neelsen staining demonstrates acid-fast mycobacteria as red bacilli in respiratory specimens.

questions.stem: Which colony/staining combination supports Streptococcus pneumoniae in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Pneumococcus is alpha-hemolytic and optochin-sensitive, with characteristic depressed colonies.

questions.stem: Which host group is at increased risk of pneumococcal pneumonia?

options.A: Only patients with skin burns but no other risk
options.B: People with no respiratory exposure ever
options.D: Only individuals with intact immune defenses

questions.explanation: Loss of splenic function increases susceptibility to pneumococcal infection.

questions.stem: Pneumonia develops at least 48 hours after hospital admission and was not incubating on admission. How is it classified?
questions.explanation: The lecture uses onset at least 48 hours after admission to describe hospital-acquired pneumonia.

questions.stem: Which intervention increases risk of hospital-acquired pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Assisted respiration and invasive airway support increase nosocomial pneumonia risk, especially with underlying illness.

questions.stem: Which organism is an important opportunistic pulmonary pathogen in AIDS?
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis is a major opportunistic cause of pneumonia in immunocompromised patients, particularly AIDS.

questions.stem: Which virus is particularly important in pneumonia after transplantation?
questions.explanation: CMV is an important opportunistic infection in transplant recipients.

questions.stem: Which occupational exposure suggests Coxiella burnetii infection?
questions.explanation: Q fever due to Coxiella is associated with farm workers and veterinarians.

questions.stem: Which specimen directly samples lower respiratory secretions through bronchoscopy?
questions.explanation: BAL obtains lower-airway material for microscopy, culture and other tests, particularly useful in immunocompromised hosts.

questions.stem: Which test can rapidly detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA?
questions.explanation: PCR amplifies mycobacterial DNA and can provide detection more rapidly than conventional slow culture.

questions.stem: Which medium is used for conventional mycobacterial culture?

options.A: Simple nutrient agar for immediate overnight confirmation

questions.explanation: Lowenstein–Jensen is a classic culture medium for M. tuberculosis; Bordet–Gengou is associated with pertussis.

questions.stem: A patient has transient pulmonary infiltrates, cough and eosinophilia during early Ascaris infection, but no stool eggs. Why are eggs absent?

options.A: Larvae are still migrating before intestinal adult maturation
options.C: All eggs are produced in pulmonary veins

questions.explanation: During the lung phase, adult egg-producing intestinal worms have not yet developed.

questions.stem: A barefoot farm worker develops itchy feet followed by cough and eosinophilia. Which infective stage best explains hookworm acquisition?
questions.explanation: Hookworm filariform larvae penetrate skin and migrate through the lungs before reaching the intestine.

questions.stem: A child exposed to soil contaminated by dog feces has eosinophilia, hepatomegaly and pulmonary symptoms. Which syndrome is likely?
questions.explanation: Toxocara larvae migrate through human tissues, producing visceral larva migrans rather than intestinal adult infection.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic schistosomiasis develops pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular hypertrophy. What causes the vascular obstruction?

options.A: Mature worms replacing all alveolar epithelium

questions.explanation: Egg granulomas obstruct pulmonary arterioles, increasing resistance and leading to cor pulmonale.

questions.stem: Weeks after schistosome exposure, fever, urticaria, hepatosplenomegaly and eosinophilia develop as egg laying starts. What is this syndrome?
questions.explanation: Acute schistosomiasis or Katayama syndrome occurs around the onset of egg deposition and antigen-driven immune reactions.

questions.stem: Which stage of Ascaris is acquired through contaminated food or water?
questions.explanation: Humans acquire Ascaris by ingesting mature embryonated eggs.

questions.stem: Where do adult Ascaris worms normally reside after pulmonary migration?
questions.explanation: Larvae migrate through lung and airway, are swallowed, and mature in the small intestine.

questions.stem: Which blood finding supports a tissue-migrating helminth infection?

options.A: Isolated thrombocytosis as a specific sign

questions.explanation: Tissue migration commonly elicits eosinophilia, especially with associated pulmonary inflammation.

questions.stem: Which intestinal effect of adult hookworms can cause anemia?

options.A: Blood feeding and mucosal blood loss
options.B: Destruction of vitamin B12 in every case
options.C: Exclusive inhibition of marrow stem cells

questions.explanation: Adult hookworms attach in the small intestine and ingest blood, producing chronic blood loss and anemia.

questions.stem: Why is routine stool egg detection not a useful way to establish human toxocariasis?

options.B: Toxocara does not mature into egg-producing adults in humans
options.D: All human infection remains in the stomach

questions.explanation: Humans harbor migrating larvae, while adult worms and egg production occur in dogs or cats.

questions.stem: Which test is used to support toxocariasis diagnosis in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Serologic ELISA supports diagnosis of tissue larval infection, including ocular disease in appropriate samples.

questions.stem: Which Toxocara complication may threaten sight?

options.B: Mechanical obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct by eggs

questions.explanation: Larvae can migrate to ocular tissues and produce damaging inflammatory lesions.

questions.stem: Which infective stage penetrates human skin in schistosomiasis?
questions.explanation: Free-swimming schistosome cercariae penetrate the skin during contaminated freshwater exposure.

questions.stem: Where are Schistosoma haematobium eggs primarily sought?
questions.explanation: S. haematobium is associated with the urogenital venous system and eggs in urine; S. mansoni eggs are sought in stool.

questions.stem: Which preventive measure specifically reduces hookworm acquisition?
questions.explanation: Shoes reduce skin contact with soil containing skin-penetrating hookworm larvae.

lecture_sets.subject: Microbiology
lecture_sets.title: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: A patient has an amoebic liver abscess followed by right-sided pleuritic pain and pulmonary disease. What is the usual route to the chest?

options.A: Rupture or extension from a right-lobe liver abscess
options.B: Inhalation of mature amoebic cysts directly into alveoli
options.D: Spread from a primary rib tumor

questions.explanation: Pleuropulmonary amoebiasis commonly follows rupture or contiguous extension of a right hepatic abscess.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: A pulmonary hydatid cyst ruptures and the patient develops severe allergy and hypotension. What explains this?

options.B: Release of antigenic cyst fluid causing anaphylaxis
options.C: Release of bacterial endotoxin from every cyst

questions.explanation: Hydatid cyst leakage can release highly antigenic material and provoke severe allergic reactions including anaphylaxis.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: After hydatid rupture, additional cysts develop in distant tissues. Which component can seed these lesions?
questions.explanation: Released protoscolices can disseminate and produce secondary echinococcosis.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: A patient with chronic bloody sputum ate undercooked freshwater crab. Acid-fast studies are negative. Which parasite is suggested?
questions.explanation: Paragonimiasis is acquired from metacercariae in freshwater crustaceans and may mimic pulmonary TB.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: Eggs of a lung fluke are detected in stool. How did they most likely reach the intestine?

options.B: Egg production by adult worms confined to the colon
options.D: Transformation of liver cells into eggs

questions.explanation: Paragonimus eggs can be coughed up and swallowed, allowing their detection in stool as well as sputum.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: Which parasite causes hydatid disease?
questions.explanation: Echinococcus granulosus is the cestode responsible for cystic echinococcosis.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: Which parasite is the oriental lung fluke?
questions.explanation: Paragonimus is a trematode that establishes pulmonary cystic lesions.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: Which stage of Paragonimus infects humans?
questions.explanation: Humans ingest metacercariae in inadequately cooked freshwater crabs or crayfish.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: Which pair represents the first and second intermediate hosts of Paragonimus?
questions.explanation: The life cycle uses a snail first and a freshwater crustacean second.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: Which stage of Entamoeba histolytica invades tissues?
questions.explanation: Ingested cysts establish infection, but trophozoites invade the bowel and can cause extraintestinal abscesses.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: What is the usual infective form of Entamoeba histolytica acquired orally?
questions.explanation: Fecal-oral ingestion of mature cysts through contaminated food, water or hands initiates infection.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: What chiefly determines pressure symptoms from an intact hydatid cyst?
questions.explanation: Slow-growing cysts can compress structures; consequences depend on location, size and burden.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: Why is unplanned aspiration of a suspected hydatid cyst hazardous?

options.A: Leakage can cause anaphylaxis and secondary seeding
options.B: It always sterilizes the cyst immediately
options.C: It transforms the parasite into a bacterium

questions.explanation: The lecture warns against diagnostic aspiration because leakage of antigenic fluid and viable material is dangerous.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: Which specimen may reveal Paragonimus eggs in pulmonary infection?

options.A: Urine as the only diagnostic sample

questions.explanation: Pulmonary cysts release eggs into airways, allowing sputum detection; swallowed eggs may appear in stool.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung

questions.stem: Which exposure-control measure most directly prevents foodborne paragonimiasis?

options.C: Thoroughly cooking freshwater crabs and crayfish
options.D: Avoiding all freshwater fish contact with skin

questions.explanation: Avoiding raw or inadequately cooked infected crustaceans interrupts metacercarial ingestion.
questions.concept: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung
