questions.stem: Which pleural layer is directly adherent to the lung and enters its fissures?
questions.explanation: Visceral pleura closely invests the lung and its fissures.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: Which opposing pleural surfaces form the costodiaphragmatic recess?

options.D: Visceral pleura of two adjacent lobes

questions.explanation: This recess is a potential space where costal pleura reflects onto the diaphragm.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: A patient has sharp, well-localized pain from inflammation of the lateral chest-wall pleura. Which nerves carry it?
questions.explanation: Somatic intercostal afferents supply the costal parietal pleura.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: Inflammation of the central diaphragmatic pleura produces shoulder pain. Which nerve accounts for the referral?
questions.explanation: Phrenic afferents enter C3–C5, sharing spinal segments with shoulder-region sensation.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: An upright patient has a small pleural effusion. Which pleural recess tends to collect this fluid inferiorly?
questions.explanation: Gravity favors fluid collection in the inferior costodiaphragmatic recess.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: Which lung surface contains the hilum?
questions.explanation: The root enters the lung at the hilum on its mediastinal surface.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: Why does the anterior border of the left lung deviate laterally near the fourth costal cartilage?

options.D: To create an additional upper lobe

questions.explanation: The left anterior border is indented by the heart, creating the cardiac notch.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: At quiet respiration, a penetrating injury at the right midclavicular line reaches the lower lung border near which rib?
questions.explanation: The inferior lung border is conventionally marked at ribs 6, 8 and 10 across the three reference lines.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: A wound just above the medial third of the clavicle causes an apical pneumothorax. Which structure projects into this area?
questions.explanation: The apex and pleural dome extend into the root of the neck above the first rib.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: What is the pulmonary ligament anatomically?

options.A: The lower edge of the oblique fissure
options.B: A double fold of mediastinal pleura below the lung root
options.C: A tendon attaching the lung apex to the clavicle
options.D: A thickened branch of the pulmonary artery

questions.answer_text: A double fold of mediastinal pleura below the lung root
questions.explanation: Pleura reflects around the root and continues inferiorly as the pulmonary ligament.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: A bronchopulmonary segment is supplied centrally by which pair?

options.C: Segmental bronchus and segmental pulmonary artery

questions.answer_text: Segmental bronchus and segmental pulmonary artery
questions.explanation: Each segment has its own segmental bronchus and pulmonary arterial branch.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: Which vessels characteristically run in planes between bronchopulmonary segments?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary veins tend to follow intersegmental planes rather than the central bronchovascular axis.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: A localized lesion is removed by segmentectomy while preserving adjacent lung. Which anatomical feature makes this possible?

options.B: A complete visceral pleural sac around every segment
options.C: A separate main bronchus for every segment
options.D: Absence of venous drainage between segments

questions.explanation: Segmental bronchi and arteries allow individual segments to be isolated surgically.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: Which fissures divide the right lung into its three lobes?
questions.explanation: The right lung has oblique and horizontal fissures; the left normally has only an oblique fissure.

source_references.title: Course material: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
NCBI Bookshelf: Anatomy of the pleurae

questions.stem: The lingula belongs to which anatomical part of the lung?
questions.explanation: The lingula is a tongue-like extension of the left upper lobe beside the cardiac notch.

questions.stem: Which property allows a hematopoietic stem cell to maintain blood-cell production throughout life?

options.B: Permanent differentiation into one granulocyte type
options.C: Division only after leaving bone marrow
options.D: Production of mature erythrocytes by fragmentation

questions.explanation: Stem cells both replenish themselves and generate progenitors for multiple blood-cell lineages.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: Which site normally contains active red marrow in a healthy adult?
questions.explanation: Adult hematopoiesis is concentrated in axial bones and selected proximal long-bone regions.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: Which cell arises through the lymphoid lineage rather than the myeloid lineage?
questions.explanation: B cells belong to the lymphoid lineage; the other listed cells arise from myeloid progenitors.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: Which organ is a major site of blood-cell formation during much of fetal life before marrow predominates?
questions.explanation: The fetal liver supports substantial hematopoiesis before bone marrow becomes the principal site.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: During normal erythroblast maturation, which paired change occurs?

options.A: Smaller cell size and increasing hemoglobin
options.B: Larger cell size and decreasing hemoglobin
options.C: Increasing nuclear size and increasing mitoses

questions.answer_text: Smaller cell size and increasing hemoglobin
questions.explanation: Erythroid cells generally become smaller, condense their nuclei and accumulate hemoglobin.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: What distinguishes a reticulocyte from a mature erythrocyte?
questions.explanation: Reticulocytes are enucleated erythroid cells retaining residual RNA during final maturation.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: A marrow smear shows a small erythroid cell with a densely condensed nucleus immediately before enucleation. Which stage is present?
questions.explanation: The orthochromatic erythroblast extrudes its pyknotic nucleus to become a reticulocyte.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease has anemia with an inappropriately low reticulocyte response. Reduced production of which hormone contributes?
questions.explanation: Reduced renal erythropoietin limits erythroid progenitor survival and red-cell production.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: Which marrow cell releases platelets as cytoplasmic fragments?
questions.explanation: Platelets derive from the cytoplasm of large marrow megakaryocytes.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: A marrow specimen contains a very large cell with abundant cytoplasm and a multilobulated polyploid nucleus. What is it?
questions.explanation: Megakaryocytes develop polyploid nuclei and abundant platelet-producing cytoplasm.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: At which granulocytic stage do lineage-specific granules first become apparent?
questions.explanation: Myelocytes first show specific granules; promyelocytes have primary azurophilic granules.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: A patient with an acute bacterial infection has increased band neutrophils. This finding most directly indicates what?

options.C: Conversion of monocytes into bands in blood
options.D: Release of less mature neutrophils from marrow

questions.answer_text: Release of less mature neutrophils from marrow
questions.explanation: A left shift reflects increased release of immature neutrophilic forms during demand.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: Several days after controlled blood loss, reticulocytes increase. What does this demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Reticulocytosis after a delay indicates increased marrow red-cell output.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: After cytotoxic chemotherapy, erythrocytes, granulocytes and platelets all fall. Which site is most directly affected?
questions.explanation: Suppression of proliferating marrow progenitors can cause multilineage cytopenias.

source_references.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Embryology, Hematopoiesis
NCBI Clinical Methods: Reticulocytes

questions.stem: Which reaction is greatly accelerated by erythrocyte carbonic anhydrase?

questions.stem: As CO₂ enters erythrocytes in systemic capillaries, which membrane exchange is expected?

options.B: Hydrogen ions leave in exchange for sodium

questions.explanation: The bicarbonate–chloride exchanger preserves electrical neutrality as bicarbonate exits the erythrocyte.

source_references.title: Course material: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood

questions.stem: A red cell reaches an alveolar capillary and unloads CO₂. How does its bicarbonate–chloride exchange change?

options.B: Both bicarbonate and chloride leave through the same exchange cycle
options.C: Chloride enters without any anion leaving

questions.explanation: The chloride shift reverses in the lungs, allowing bicarbonate to supply CO₂ for exhalation.

source_references.title: Course material: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood

questions.stem: Which molecule buffers much of the H⁺ generated when CO₂ enters an erythrocyte?

source_references.title: Course material: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood

questions.stem: CO₂ forming carbaminohemoglobin binds primarily to which part of hemoglobin?

options.C: The oxygen-binding pocket on heme iron

source_references.title: Course material: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood

questions.stem: Venous blood can carry more CO₂ at a given PCO₂ than oxygenated arterial blood. Which effect explains this?
questions.explanation: Deoxygenated hemoglobin has a greater capacity to carry CO₂ and buffer H⁺.

source_references.title: Course material: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood

questions.stem: An active muscle raises local CO₂ and H⁺. Hemoglobin then releases oxygen more readily. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Higher CO₂ and acidity reduce hemoglobin oxygen affinity and promote tissue unloading.

source_references.title: Course material: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood

questions.stem: Why does oxygenation of hemoglobin in the lungs help release CO₂?

options.A: It reduces hemoglobin binding of CO₂ and H⁺
options.B: It prevents bicarbonate entry into erythrocytes
options.C: It converts globin into carbonic anhydrase
options.D: It increases carbamino binding at unchanged PCO₂

questions.answer_text: It reduces hemoglobin binding of CO₂ and H⁺
questions.explanation: Oxygenation releases H⁺ and decreases carbamino binding, supporting pulmonary CO₂ unloading.

source_references.title: Course material: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood

questions.stem: During pulmonary CO₂ unloading, H⁺ released from hemoglobin combines with bicarbonate. What gas is ultimately produced?
questions.explanation: Bicarbonate and H⁺ regenerate carbonic acid, which becomes CO₂ and water.

questions.stem: Why is a greater fraction of blood CO₂ than oxygen carried physically dissolved?

options.A: CO₂ occupies all heme oxygen-binding sites

questions.explanation: Greater CO₂ solubility supports a larger dissolved component than for oxygen.

source_references.title: Course material: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood

questions.stem: An erythrocyte exporting newly formed bicarbonate must avoid accumulating net positive charge. Which process serves this function?

options.B: Active export of every intracellular proton
options.D: Entry of chloride through an anion exchanger

questions.explanation: The chloride shift exchanges one anion for another and supports electroneutrality.

source_references.title: Course material: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Bohr and Haldane effects?

options.A: Bohr concerns O₂ affinity; Haldane concerns CO₂ carrying with oxygenation state
options.B: Bohr concerns platelet aggregation; Haldane concerns oxygen diffusion
options.C: Both refer only to chloride movement
options.D: Both require CO₂ to bind heme iron

questions.answer_text: Bohr concerns O₂ affinity; Haldane concerns CO₂ carrying with oxygenation state
questions.explanation: The Bohr effect alters oxygen affinity, while the Haldane effect links oxygenation to CO₂ carriage.

source_references.title: Course material: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood

questions.stem: A small tissue-to-lung PCO₂ difference can unload substantial CO₂ because the physiological CO₂-content curve is relatively what?

source_references.title: Course material: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood

questions.stem: Blood entering an alveolar capillary has PCO₂ above alveolar PCO₂. What directly drives CO₂ into the alveolus?

options.D: Binding of CO₂ to surfactant proteins

questions.explanation: CO₂ diffuses from higher blood partial pressure toward lower alveolar partial pressure.

questions.stem: The primary automatic respiratory control centers lie mainly in which brainstem region?

questions.stem: In the lecture's respiratory-center model, which group supplies the principal inspiratory drive during quiet breathing?
questions.explanation: The dorsal respiratory group contains predominantly inspiratory neurons supplying inspiratory motor pathways.

questions.stem: Which activity most clearly recruits the ventral respiratory group's expiratory neurons?

options.B: Passive recoil after a normal tidal inspiration
options.D: Relaxation of the diaphragm at quiet rest

questions.explanation: The ventral group contributes to increased ventilatory demand and active expiratory muscle recruitment.

source_references.title: Course material: Neural control of breathing

questions.stem: Which neuronal network is especially associated with generating the basic inspiratory rhythm?
questions.explanation: The pre-Bötzinger complex contains rhythm-generating respiratory networks.

source_references.title: Course material: Neural control of breathing

questions.stem: Stronger inspiratory off-switch activity from the upper pons tends to do what?

options.C: Remove inhibitory feedback from lung inflation
options.D: Increase the duration of the inspiratory ramp

source_references.title: Course material: Neural control of breathing

questions.stem: Following brainstem injury, inspiration becomes prolonged and gasping, with brief expirations. What breathing pattern is this?
questions.explanation: Apneusis consists of prolonged inspiratory efforts interrupted by brief expiration.

source_references.title: Course material: Neural control of breathing

questions.stem: A singer deliberately holds a note by modifying expiration. Which higher center chiefly provides voluntary control?
questions.explanation: Cortical motor pathways allow voluntary respiratory maneuvers such as speech and singing.

source_references.title: Course material: Neural control of breathing

questions.stem: During voluntary breath holding, rising arterial CO₂ eventually forces breathing to resume. Which process chiefly opposes the voluntary command?

options.A: Progressive suppression of all respiratory neurons
options.C: A fall in tissue CO₂ production to zero

source_references.title: Course material: Neural control of breathing

questions.stem: An unusually large inspiration activates pulmonary stretch receptors that inhibit further inspiration. Which reflex is responsible?
questions.explanation: Lung inflation activates stretch-receptor feedback that limits further inspiratory activity.

source_references.title: Course material: Neural control of breathing

questions.stem: Pulmonary stretch-receptor feedback reaches the brainstem mainly through which nerve?
questions.explanation: Vagal afferents carry pulmonary stretch information to respiratory control networks.

source_references.title: Course material: Neural control of breathing

questions.stem: At the onset of exercise, moving muscles and joints send signals that increase ventilation. Which receptor group contributes?

source_references.title: Course material: Neural control of breathing

questions.stem: What best describes the relationship between pontine and medullary respiratory centers?

options.A: Pontine centers directly supply every respiratory muscle motor end plate
options.B: Medullary centers function only during voluntary breathing
options.C: The pons is the primary peripheral sensor of arterial PO₂
options.D: Pontine centers fine-tune the medullary breathing pattern

questions.answer_text: Pontine centers fine-tune the medullary breathing pattern
questions.explanation: The pons modifies medullary output to coordinate the timing and transitions of breathing.

source_references.title: Course material: Neural control of breathing

questions.stem: An anxious person begins breathing rapidly despite no immediate increase in muscle metabolism. Which higher-center influence can contribute?

source_references.title: Course material: Neural control of breathing

questions.stem: Respiratory muscles need neural input to breathe rhythmically because their skeletal muscle fibers normally lack what?

questions.explanation: Brainstem networks provide rhythmic motor commands to skeletal respiratory muscles.

source_references.title: Course material: Neural control of breathing

questions.stem: Why must sensory feedback modify the basic respiratory rhythm?

options.A: To keep ventilation fixed regardless of metabolism
options.B: To prevent all voluntary respiratory control
options.C: To match ventilation to changing physiological demands
options.D: To remove the need for respiratory motor neurons

questions.answer_text: To match ventilation to changing physiological demands
questions.explanation: A fixed rhythm alone cannot account for changes in metabolism, lung inflation and behavior.

questions.stem: Which immediate chemical signal directly stimulates central respiratory chemoreceptors?

options.B: Reduced oxygen content with unchanged PaO₂

questions.explanation: Central chemoreceptors respond to local acidity, strongly influenced by CO₂ entering the brain.

questions.stem: Why does arterial CO₂ strongly stimulate central chemoreceptors?

options.A: Plasma H⁺ crosses the barrier much faster than CO₂
options.B: CO₂ crosses into CSF and generates H⁺
options.C: CO₂ binds directly to carotid-body hemoglobin
options.D: CO₂ prevents all CSF acid formation

questions.answer_text: CO₂ crosses into CSF and generates H⁺
questions.explanation: Diffusible CO₂ generates hydrogen ions in CSF, linking arterial PCO₂ to central stimulation.

source_references.title: Course material: Chemical control of breathing

questions.stem: Where are the principal peripheral respiratory chemoreceptors?

options.B: A rise in PaCO₂ with increased CSF H⁺
options.C: A fall in CSF pH despite normal arterial PO₂
options.D: A marked reduction in arterial PO₂

questions.answer_text: A marked reduction in arterial PO₂
questions.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors detect low arterial PO₂; central receptors do not directly sense hypoxemia.

source_references.title: Course material: Chemical control of breathing

questions.stem: A patient with metabolic acidosis develops deep, rapid breathing. Which receptor input directly detects the increased arterial H⁺?

options.B: Central chemoreceptors directly responding to plasma H⁺
options.C: Pulmonary stretch receptors responding to acid in arterial blood
options.D: Carotid sinus baroreceptors detecting bicarbonate loss

source_references.title: Course material: Chemical control of breathing

questions.stem: After acute hypoventilation, PaCO₂ rises. What immediate ventilatory response is expected if respiratory control is intact?

options.C: Selective slowing of ventilation to retain more CO₂

source_references.title: Course material: Chemical control of breathing

questions.stem: An otherwise healthy person voluntarily hyperventilates, lowering PaCO₂. What happens to the chemical drive to breathe afterward?

questions.stem: Why may severe anemia fail to strongly activate the hypoxic peripheral chemoreceptor response?

options.C: Oxygen content and oxygen tension are identical variables

questions.stem: A patient has carbon-monoxide poisoning with low usable oxygen content but preserved PaO₂. Why can the expected hypoxic ventilatory stimulus be limited?

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve carries carotid-body chemoreceptor signals to the brainstem?

questions.stem: Aortic-body chemoreceptor afferents reach the medulla predominantly through which nerve?

source_references.title: Course material: Chemical control of breathing

questions.stem: Soon after ascent to high altitude, a healthy person increases ventilation. What initiates the hypoxic component of this response?

options.A: Higher arterial oxygen content stimulating central receptors
options.B: Increased plasma H⁺ from retained CO₂ in every case
options.C: Direct stimulation of pulmonary stretch receptors by low pressure
options.D: Reduced arterial PO₂ stimulating peripheral chemoreceptors

questions.answer_text: Reduced arterial PO₂ stimulating peripheral chemoreceptors
questions.explanation: Lower inspired oxygen pressure reduces PaO₂ and activates the peripheral hypoxic response.

source_references.title: Course material: Chemical control of breathing

questions.stem: How does increased alveolar ventilation counter an acute rise in PaCO₂?

options.B: It directly increases metabolic CO₂ production

questions.explanation: Greater alveolar ventilation removes more CO₂ and opposes the initiating chemical disturbance.

options.D: Inability of CO₂ to cross the blood–brain barrier

questions.answer_text: Reduced central sensitivity compared with the initial CO₂ rise

source_references.title: Course material: Chemical control of breathing

questions.stem: Which combination tends to increase peripheral chemoreceptor firing?

options.A: High PaO₂, low PaCO₂ and reduced arterial H⁺

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes hypoxemia from tissue hypoxia?

options.A: Hypoxemia is low arterial PO₂; hypoxia is inadequate tissue oxygen availability or use
options.C: Hypoxia always requires low arterial PO₂
options.D: Hypoxemia means low venous blood pressure

questions.answer_text: Hypoxemia is low arterial PO₂; hypoxia is inadequate tissue oxygen availability or use
questions.explanation: Tissue oxygen failure can occur with normal PaO₂, as in anemia, low flow or impaired cellular utilization.

source_references.title: Course material: Hypoxia and cyanosis

NCBI Bookshelf: Central and Peripheral Cyanosis

questions.stem: Which situation most directly produces hypoxic hypoxia?

options.A: Isolated severe anemia with normal lungs
options.B: Low inspired oxygen pressure at altitude
options.C: Isolated low cardiac output with normal arterial gases

questions.answer_text: Low inspired oxygen pressure at altitude
questions.explanation: Low inspired oxygen reduces arterial oxygen tension and can cause hypoxic hypoxia.

source_references.title: Course material: Hypoxia and cyanosis

NCBI Bookshelf: Central and Peripheral Cyanosis

questions.stem: A patient has hemoglobin 5 g/dL, normal PaO₂ and tissue oxygen deficiency. Which type of hypoxia is present?

options.A: Hypoxic hypoxia from low inspired oxygen

source_references.title: Course material: Hypoxia and cyanosis

NCBI Bookshelf: Central and Peripheral Cyanosis

questions.stem: Cardiogenic shock reduces tissue oxygen delivery despite normal arterial PO₂. Which mechanism dominates?

options.A: Failure of oxygen to bind all normal hemoglobin

source_references.title: Course material: Hypoxia and cyanosis
NCBI Bookshelf: Hypoxia
NCBI Bookshelf: Central and Peripheral Cyanosis

questions.stem: After cyanide exposure, cells cannot use delivered oxygen normally. Which hypoxia category best fits?

source_references.title: Course material: Hypoxia and cyanosis

NCBI Bookshelf: Central and Peripheral Cyanosis

questions.stem: Which hypoxia type can leave venous oxygen unusually high because extraction is impaired?

options.D: Uncompensated anemic hypoxia in every case

source_references.title: Course material: Hypoxia and cyanosis

NCBI Bookshelf: Central and Peripheral Cyanosis

questions.stem: Visible cyanosis primarily reflects increased capillary concentration of which substance?
questions.explanation: Cyanosis is the bluish appearance associated with sufficient deoxygenated hemoglobin in superficial blood.

questions.stem: A severely anemic patient is profoundly hypoxic but not visibly cyanosed. What best explains this?

options.B: Anemia always prevents tissue oxygen extraction
options.C: Absence of cyanosis proves adequate oxygen delivery
options.D: Too little total hemoglobin to accumulate enough deoxygenated hemoglobin

questions.answer_text: Too little total hemoglobin to accumulate enough deoxygenated hemoglobin
questions.explanation: Cyanosis depends on the absolute amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin and can be absent in severe anemia.

source_references.title: Course material: Hypoxia and cyanosis

NCBI Bookshelf: Central and Peripheral Cyanosis

questions.stem: Why can cyanosis be more apparent in polycythemia than anemia at a similar oxygen saturation?

options.A: More total hemoglobin permits more deoxygenated hemoglobin
options.C: Cyanosis depends only on platelet count
options.D: Polycythemia always causes lower inspired PO₂

questions.answer_text: More total hemoglobin permits more deoxygenated hemoglobin
questions.explanation: A higher hemoglobin concentration increases the absolute deoxygenated fraction at a given saturation.

source_references.title: Course material: Hypoxia and cyanosis

NCBI Bookshelf: Central and Peripheral Cyanosis

questions.stem: Which finding most strongly supports central rather than isolated peripheral cyanosis?

options.A: Cold blue fingertips with a pink tongue
options.C: Blue toes improving promptly with warming
options.D: A blue hand distal to local venous obstruction

NCBI Bookshelf: Central and Peripheral Cyanosis

questions.stem: A person has cold blue fingers but a pink tongue and normal arterial oxygen saturation. What is the likely mechanism?

questions.explanation: Cold-related vasoconstriction increases extraction in peripheral capillaries without requiring arterial desaturation.

source_references.title: Course material: Hypoxia and cyanosis

NCBI Bookshelf: Central and Peripheral Cyanosis

questions.stem: Why can warming improve peripheral cyanosis caused by cold exposure?

options.B: It abolishes all tissue oxygen consumption

options.D: It increases local blood flow and reduces excessive extraction per unit blood

questions.answer_text: It increases local blood flow and reduces excessive extraction per unit blood

source_references.title: Course material: Hypoxia and cyanosis

NCBI Bookshelf: Central and Peripheral Cyanosis

questions.stem: With normal saturation, which change most directly lowers arterial oxygen content?

options.C: Increased plasma sodium with unchanged hemoglobin

questions.stem: Tissue oxygen delivery is most directly determined by arterial oxygen content multiplied by what?

questions.answer_text: Mixing deoxygenated venous blood into systemic arterial blood

questions.stem: Which conversion is promoted by ACE on the pulmonary capillary endothelium?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary endothelial ACE activates angiotensin I and also degrades bradykinin.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: A patient develops a dry cough after an ACE inhibitor. Reduced degradation of which pulmonary peptide contributes?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibition can increase bradykinin, contributing to the characteristic dry cough.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: Which phospholipid provides the major low-surface-tension component of pulmonary surfactant?
questions.explanation: Saturated DPPC packs tightly at the alveolar interface and supplies strong surface activity.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: How do surfactant phospholipids orient at the alveolar air–liquid interface?

options.A: Hydrophobic tails toward fluid and heads toward air
options.B: Both heads and tails entirely within the alveolar cell nucleus
options.C: All molecules dissolved only in the capillary plasma
options.D: Hydrophilic heads toward fluid and hydrophobic tails toward air

questions.answer_text: Hydrophilic heads toward fluid and hydrophobic tails toward air
questions.explanation: Amphipathic phospholipids organize at the interface to disrupt water's cohesive surface forces.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: Surfactant is stored before secretion mainly in which organelles?

options.A: Lamellar bodies of type II pneumocytes
options.B: Secretory granules of airway goblet cells

questions.answer_text: Lamellar bodies of type II pneumocytes
questions.explanation: Type II cells package surfactant in lamellar bodies for regulated exocytosis.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: Which surfactant protein pair is especially associated with innate immune recognition?
questions.explanation: SP-A and SP-D are hydrophilic collectins involved in host defense.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: Which protein pair chiefly supports surfactant adsorption, spreading and film stability?
questions.explanation: Hydrophobic SP-B and SP-C organize phospholipids and support a functional surface film.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: Two model alveoli have equal surface tension, but one has half the radius. What pressure is needed to keep the smaller one open?
questions.explanation: In the simplified spherical model, P=2T/r, so halving radius doubles required pressure at constant tension.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: A premature infant develops diffuse atelectasis and poor lung compliance shortly after birth. Which biochemical deficiency best explains this?
questions.explanation: An immature surfactant system raises surface tension, promoting collapse and low compliance.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: An infant has inherited SP-B deficiency and severe respiratory failure. Which surfactant function is most directly impaired?

options.B: Formation and stability of the phospholipid surface film
options.C: Active absorption of alveolar sodium by type I cells
options.D: Diffusion of dissolved oxygen through the capillary plasma

questions.answer_text: Formation and stability of the phospholipid surface film
questions.explanation: SP-B is essential for normal surfactant film organization and function.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: In ARDS, protein-rich alveolar fluid can worsen collapse through what surfactant-related effect?

options.D: Selective acceleration of functional DPPC respreading

questions.explanation: Leakage and inflammation can impair surfactant and increase alveolar instability.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: Antenatal corticosteroids promote fetal lung maturation primarily by enhancing which process?

options.C: Replacement of alveolar epithelium with cartilage
options.D: Type II cell maturation and surfactant synthesis

questions.answer_text: Type II cell maturation and surfactant synthesis
questions.explanation: Glucocorticoids accelerate the biochemical machinery of surfactant production when clinically indicated.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: Why is sphingomyelin used as a comparator in the traditional amniotic-fluid lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio?

options.A: It is relatively stable while lecithin increases with maturity
options.B: It rises more steeply than lecithin throughout late gestation
options.C: It is absent from all immature lungs
options.D: It is the principal surface-active surfactant protein

questions.answer_text: It is relatively stable while lecithin increases with maturity
questions.explanation: A rising lecithin concentration relative to more stable sphingomyelin forms the basis of this historical marker.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: An amniotic-fluid test detects phosphatidylglycerol. What does this generally support?

options.A: Absence of a fetal surfactant pool
options.B: Greater biochemical maturity of the surfactant system
options.C: Early rather than late phospholipid maturation
options.D: A direct measurement of fetal arterial oxygen tension

questions.answer_text: Greater biochemical maturity of the surfactant system
questions.explanation: Phosphatidylglycerol appears relatively late and has historically supported assessment of fetal lung maturity.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: Why can amniotic-fluid lamellar-body counting reflect surfactant maturity?

options.A: They are nuclei shed by fetal erythrocytes
options.B: They measure fetal arterial oxygen directly
options.C: Lamellar bodies are surfactant-storage particles released into fetal lung fluid
options.D: They are aggregates of pulmonary capillary platelets

questions.answer_text: Lamellar bodies are surfactant-storage particles released into fetal lung fluid
questions.explanation: The count estimates surfactant-containing particles; interpretation depends on laboratory method and context.

source_references.title: Course material: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant

questions.stem: Which substance represents the principal volatile acid load eliminated through the lungs?
questions.explanation: The lungs regulate the volatile CO₂/carbonic-acid component, whereas nonvolatile acid handling requires other pathways.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: Blood pH in the bicarbonate system depends most directly on which ratio?
questions.explanation: The Henderson–Hasselbalch relationship links pH to bicarbonate relative to the CO₂ component.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: Which erythrocyte protein contributes importantly to buffering H⁺ produced from CO₂ hydration?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin's ionizable groups buffer hydrogen ions inside red cells.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: A patient with opioid-induced hypoventilation has pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 60 mmHg and bicarbonate 26 mmol/L. What is the primary disorder?
questions.explanation: Low pH with a primary elevation of PaCO₂ indicates respiratory acidosis.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: During acute anxiety-related hyperventilation, pH is 7.52, PaCO₂ 28 mmHg and bicarbonate 23 mmol/L. What is the primary disturbance?
questions.explanation: A low PaCO₂ accompanying alkalemia identifies a primary respiratory alkalosis.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: A patient has pH 7.28, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L and PaCO₂ 26 mmHg. Which interpretation is best?
questions.explanation: Reduced bicarbonate is the primary acidifying change; lower PaCO₂ reflects compensatory ventilation.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: After repeated vomiting, a patient has pH 7.50, bicarbonate 36 mmol/L and PaCO₂ 48 mmHg. What is the principal disorder?
questions.explanation: High bicarbonate explains alkalemia; a compensatory rise in PaCO₂ partly opposes it.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: If CO₂ production stays constant and alveolar ventilation doubles, PaCO₂ tends to do what?

options.D: Fall to about half its previous value

questions.answer_text: Fall to about half its previous value
questions.explanation: At stable production, arterial PCO₂ varies inversely with alveolar ventilation.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: Why does hypoventilation lower blood pH?

options.A: Retained CO₂ increases the carbonic-acid component
options.B: It removes all plasma bicarbonate immediately
options.C: It selectively eliminates hydrogen ions through the lung
options.D: It always reduces CO₂ production to zero

questions.answer_text: Retained CO₂ increases the carbonic-acid component
questions.explanation: Inadequate ventilation retains CO₂, shifting the bicarbonate buffer toward greater acidity.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis develops Kussmaul breathing. What does this breathing pattern accomplish?

options.B: Lowering PaCO₂ to partly oppose metabolic acidemia
options.C: Removing ketoacids intact through the alveoli
options.D: Completely normalizing pH without treating the metabolic cause

questions.answer_text: Lowering PaCO₂ to partly oppose metabolic acidemia
questions.explanation: Increased ventilation lowers the respiratory acid component but does not remove the underlying metabolic process.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: In sustained respiratory acidosis, which renal response is expected?

options.A: Reduced bicarbonate retention in every case
options.C: Increased bicarbonate retention and net acid excretion
options.D: Selective loss of all sodium without water

questions.answer_text: Increased bicarbonate retention and net acid excretion
questions.explanation: The kidneys compensate over time by increasing bicarbonate availability and acid excretion.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: Why does chronic respiratory acidosis often have a higher bicarbonate concentration than an acute episode at the same PaCO₂?

options.A: CO₂ cannot cross the blood–brain barrier in chronic disease
options.C: All chronic respiratory acidosis is actually metabolic alkalosis
options.D: Renal compensation has had time to develop

questions.answer_text: Renal compensation has had time to develop
questions.explanation: Renal compensation develops more slowly than immediate chemical buffering.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: Why can a buffer limit a sudden pH change without eliminating the underlying acid load?

options.A: It temporarily binds or releases H⁺
options.B: It permanently destroys all hydrogen atoms
options.C: It replaces renal and respiratory regulation completely
options.D: It raises pH regardless of the initial disturbance

questions.answer_text: It temporarily binds or releases H⁺
questions.explanation: Buffers resist changes in free H⁺; excretion or correction of the cause is still needed.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: A patient has pH 7.10, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L and PaCO₂ 40 mmHg. Why is isolated compensated metabolic acidosis unlikely?

options.A: The bicarbonate is too high to indicate metabolic acidosis
options.B: PaCO₂ is not appropriately reduced, suggesting additional respiratory acidosis
options.D: A normal PaCO₂ always proves normal ventilation for the metabolic state

questions.answer_text: PaCO₂ is not appropriately reduced, suggesting additional respiratory acidosis
questions.explanation: Metabolic acidosis should lower PaCO₂; an inappropriately high value suggests a mixed disturbance.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: Why is compensatory hypoventilation in metabolic alkalosis limited?

options.A: The lungs cannot retain any CO₂
options.D: The kidneys immediately stop all oxygen consumption

questions.explanation: Excessive reduction of ventilation lowers arterial oxygen and recruits a counteracting ventilatory stimulus.

source_references.title: Course material: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system

questions.stem: A smoker develops recurrent respiratory infections after prolonged ciliary dysfunction. Which defense is most directly impaired?

questions.stem: A macrophage TLR recognizes bacterial LPS. What is LPS acting as in this interaction?

source_references.title: Course material: Lung immunology:Innate & acquired immune responses in respiratory infections

questions.stem: Why is restrained macrophage activity valuable in uninfected alveoli?

options.B: It converts alveoli into sterile lymph nodes

source_references.title: Course material: Lung immunology:Innate & acquired immune responses in respiratory infections

questions.stem: During bacterial pneumonia, macrophage chemokines recruit which cells rapidly from blood?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are rapidly recruited innate effectors that phagocytose and kill bacteria.

source_references.title: Course material: Lung immunology:Innate & acquired immune responses in respiratory infections

questions.stem: Excessive neutrophil ROS and protease release in the lung can cause which consequence?

questions.stem: Which event most directly links airway innate recognition to activation of naïve T cells?

options.D: Macrophage destruction of all captured antigen before presentation

source_references.title: Course material: Lung immunology:Innate & acquired immune responses in respiratory infections

questions.stem: A respiratory epithelial cell contains replicating influenza virus. Which adaptive cell recognizes its viral peptide on MHC I?

options.A: CD4⁺ helper T cell through MHC II
options.C: Naïve B cell through a T-cell receptor

source_references.title: Course material: Lung immunology:Innate & acquired immune responses in respiratory infections

questions.stem: Early in a viral infection, an infected cell reduces MHC I expression. Which innate lymphocyte may kill it?
questions.explanation: NK cells integrate reduced self-MHC and activating stress signals without prior antigen-specific priming.

source_references.title: Course material: Lung immunology:Innate & acquired immune responses in respiratory infections

questions.stem: Which antibody is especially suited to blocking pathogen attachment at the airway mucosal surface?

source_references.title: Course material: Lung immunology:Innate & acquired immune responses in respiratory infections

questions.stem: Why does IgG remain important in respiratory infection despite the role of secretory IgA?

options.A: It is the only antibody transported with a secretory component
options.C: It neutralizes and opsonizes organisms in tissue and lower-airway compartments

questions.answer_text: It neutralizes and opsonizes organisms in tissue and lower-airway compartments
questions.explanation: IgG contributes to neutralization, opsonization and complement-related defense beyond the mucus surface.

source_references.title: Course material: Lung immunology:Innate & acquired immune responses in respiratory infections

questions.stem: A patient with markedly reduced CD4 cells is vulnerable to tuberculosis. Which protective interaction is impaired?

options.B: Complement lysis as the principal intracellular killing mechanism
options.C: Antibody neutralization inside the macrophage cytosol
options.D: Th1 cytokine activation of infected macrophages

questions.answer_text: Th1 cytokine activation of infected macrophages
questions.explanation: CD4 Th1 responses, including IFN-γ, help macrophages contain intracellular mycobacteria.

source_references.title: Course material: Lung immunology:Innate & acquired immune responses in respiratory infections

questions.stem: How do CD4 helper T cells support B-cell responses to respiratory antigens?

options.A: Costimulatory contact and cytokines promote class switching and memory
options.B: They convert B cells directly into neutrophils
options.C: They remove immunoglobulin genes from B cells
options.D: They replace B-cell antigen recognition with hemoglobin binding

questions.answer_text: Costimulatory contact and cytokines promote class switching and memory
questions.explanation: Helper signals support effective plasma-cell responses, antibody class switching and memory formation.

source_references.title: Course material: Lung immunology:Innate & acquired immune responses in respiratory infections

questions.stem: After vaccination, exposure to the same respiratory antigen produces a faster, stronger antibody response. What accounts for this?

options.C: New receptor rearrangement only after repeat exposure
options.D: Loss of antigen specificity after vaccination

questions.explanation: Vaccination establishes adaptive memory that reduces the delay and improves the quality of later responses.

source_references.title: Course material: Lung immunology:Innate & acquired immune responses in respiratory infections

questions.stem: Why can a respiratory vaccine reduce disease severity even if infection still occurs?

options.A: Vaccines must prevent every entry event to have benefit
options.B: Vaccination permanently removes the need for innate defense
options.C: Earlier memory responses limit pathogen replication and tissue injury
options.D: Memory cells increase viral replication before clearance

questions.answer_text: Earlier memory responses limit pathogen replication and tissue injury
questions.explanation: Faster effective immunity can reduce pathogen burden and inflammatory damage without guaranteeing sterilizing immunity.

options.B: Permanent alveolar wall destruction without airway inflammation

source_references.title: CDC: Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis

questions.stem: A throat specimen is needed for suspected streptococcal pharyngitis. Which site should be sampled?
questions.explanation: A properly collected throat swab samples the infected pharyngeal and tonsillar region while minimizing oral contamination.

source_references.title: CDC: Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis

questions.stem: Which test can rapidly identify group A streptococcal antigen from a throat swab?

options.A: An antistreptolysin-O titer as a test for the current acute throat infection
options.C: An acid-fast stain of the swab
options.D: A heterophile-antibody test for every group A strep case

questions.explanation: A rapid antigen test targets group A strep; culture is another diagnostic method.

source_references.title: CDC: Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis

questions.stem: A patient has confirmed group A streptococcal pharyngitis and no penicillin allergy. Which listed drug is a standard first-line option?
questions.explanation: Penicillin or amoxicillin is recommended for susceptible patients with confirmed group A strep pharyngitis.

source_references.title: CDC: Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis

questions.stem: Why are antibiotics not routinely indicated for an uncomplicated viral cold?

options.A: They invariably worsen arterial oxygen binding
options.B: Every cold is caused by resistant bacteria
options.C: They permanently suppress all vaccine responses
options.D: They do not act against the causative viruses

questions.answer_text: They do not act against the causative viruses
questions.explanation: Antibacterial drugs do not treat an uncomplicated viral infection and unnecessary use adds adverse effects and resistance pressure.

source_references.title: CDC: Adult Outpatient Respiratory Infection Guidance

questions.stem: After initial improvement from a cold, a patient develops worsening fever and facial pain. Which pattern supports bacterial sinusitis?

options.A: Worsening after an initially improving viral illness
options.B: Rhinorrhea for one day without deterioration
options.D: A normal examination with no respiratory symptoms

questions.answer_text: Worsening after an initially improving viral illness
questions.explanation: Double worsening is one clinical pattern that raises suspicion for secondary bacterial rhinosinusitis.

source_references.title: CDC: Adult Outpatient Respiratory Infection Guidance

questions.stem: A student has fever, pharyngitis and conjunctivitis during an outbreak. Which virus is classically associated with this combination?
questions.explanation: Adenovirus can cause pharyngoconjunctival illness and respiratory outbreaks.

source_references.title: CDC: About Adenovirus

questions.stem: Abrupt fever, marked myalgia and cough during a seasonal outbreak most strongly suggest which infection?
questions.explanation: Influenza typically causes acute systemic symptoms along with respiratory illness.

source_references.title: CDC: Influenza Signs and Symptoms

questions.stem: A firmly adherent pharyngeal pseudomembrane that bleeds when disturbed raises concern for which organism?
questions.explanation: Respiratory diphtheria can produce an adherent pseudomembrane and toxin-mediated disease.

source_references.title: CDC: Clinical Guidance for Diphtheria

questions.stem: Why is diphtheria antitoxin time-sensitive in suspected respiratory diphtheria?

options.A: It neutralizes circulating toxin before tissue binding
options.B: It reverses all toxin already internalized into cells
options.C: It replaces every need for antibiotics and airway assessment

questions.answer_text: It neutralizes circulating toxin before tissue binding
questions.explanation: Antitoxin acts on unbound toxin; established intracellular toxin injury cannot simply be reversed by it.

source_references.title: CDC: Clinical Guidance for Diphtheria

questions.stem: What protective response is the diphtheria toxoid vaccine chiefly designed to generate?

options.A: Antibodies that remove all respiratory commensals
options.C: Universal immunity to every sore-throat virus
options.D: Permanent elimination of the need for boosters

questions.explanation: Toxoid immunization induces antitoxin immunity rather than universal protection against respiratory pathogens.

source_references.title: CDC: Clinical Guidance for Diphtheria

questions.stem: Treating confirmed group A strep pharyngitis helps reduce the risk of which nonsuppurative complication?

options.B: All cases of postinfectious glomerulonephritis with certainty
options.D: Every form of congenital heart disease

questions.explanation: Appropriate treatment reduces acute rheumatic fever risk; prevention of every possible complication is not guaranteed.
